Mr. Speaker, when the House rose at six o'clock I was speaking of the protection afforded to special interests in their actual or attempted monopoly of Canadian trade and markets. Let, me now come to the bestowal of favours in another direction. Mr. Murdoik has exposed the manner in which, as n-spects the necessaries of life, the food, the clothing, the articles required for the shelter of the people, associated businesse

, with their trade agreements, combines, and monopolies, have been permitted, with the assistance of a protective tariff, and to the detriment of consumers, to reap their excessive profits through unrestrained freedom of action. Let me now direct the attention of the House to the manner in which, through the interweaving of business associations and interlocking of directorates as respects a different class of enterprises, the Government has, at great cost to the taxpayers of Canada, accorded a privileged position to another few of its wealthy friends.
The two classes of expenditure most severely criticised in this House and throughout the country to-day are the expenditures on account of the Canadian National railways and the Government merchant marine. They are the two classes of expenditure about which the representatives of the people in this Parliament have been able to obtain the least information. The public know that freight and passenger rates have been increased; they know that last year there was a deficit on the national railways amounting to $48,242,536.65; that this year there is a further deficit estimated at $70,331,734.88; and that, despite the increase of rates, the deficit estimated for the ensuing year will in all probability be in the neighbourhood of $100,000,000. They know, too, that despite repeated protests, and without due regard for either the law or customary practice, $70,000,000 has been spent on the construction of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. They are aware that, as respects the latter, contracts were awarded by the Government without calling for tender; that the work of construction was distributed by the Government among its friends from the

Atlantic to the Pacific; that in many cases the contracts had been awarded, and the work permitted to get under way before the money for the purpose had been appropriated by Parliament.
The condition, however, of which the public is not as yet fully seized is the significance of the methods devised by the Government for permitting to a few of its wealthy friends a free hand in the awarding of contracts with public moneys, and claiming for itself immunity from all responsibility to Parliament and the people for enormous outlays of public moneys in the work of construction and operation of these vast systems of transportation by land and sea.
What have hon. gentlemen opposite attempted to do in the various discussions that have taken place in regard to these enormous deficits? They have talked about the increases that have been paid to the labour on the road, and throughout this country a great deal of publicity has been given to the wages that are being paid to the workingmen. Well, the Government talk about protecting labour. < Let the people's representatives in this Parliament get the facts, let us find out the truth in respect of these contracts-how they are being awarded, whom they are going to, and the prices paid, and labour will be able to take care of itself. We wish to protect labour just as much as hon. gentlemen opposite, but our methods are somewhat different. We believe the best protection that can be afforded any group of people in this country is the protection which comes from ample publicity in dealing with public affairs, not from concealment.
Talk of the super-organization of business, of the interweaving of financial, manufacturing, transportation, and distributing interests-I venture to say that never in the history of the world has a scheme been devised so well calculated to make interweaving and interlocking of private interests complete, or to permit, on so unlimited a scale, and in a manner so whol'y indefensible, the use of public moneys to augment private fortunes at the expense of the state.
What is the method to which I allude? For clearness of understanding as to its significance, let me present, by way of contrast, the method that has hitherto obtained in the management, operation, and control of like enterprises by the Government of this country; the method, for example, that obtained formerly in the management of the Intercolonial railway

and that obtains to-day under the Post Office Department. In both the latter instances, we have the doctrine of ministerial responsibility to Parliament for all that pertains to the management, operation, and control of a government enterprise, fully recognized and adhered to. In everything, the right to the fullest publicity is maintained. Contracts awarded are awarded in accordance with terms and conditions prescribed by law. Parliament looks to the minister, and the minister expects Parliament to look to him, for an accounting of every cent of public money expended under his direction, the names of the persons to whom the contracts have been awarded, the manner in which, and the terms on which, the awards have been made, the prices paid, and so forth and so forth. In other words, it is recognized that public moneys are being expended, that they are held in trust by the ministers of the departments concerned, and that the public is entitled to be satisfied in its mind both as to the necessity for, and the economies exercised in, the transactions pertaining thereto.
Compare this now with the methods devised by the present Administration in the expenditure of public moneys on those vast transportation systems. Both in the case of the Canadian National railway and the merchant marine, the Government has constituted boards of management. These boards are composed almost exclusively of the Government's own friends; almost without exception the gentlemen who compose these boards are associated with large industrial enterprises and businesses which are engaged in the manufacture, selling and distribution of the equipment and supplies required by these Government undertakings. In the awarding of contracts, they are given a perfectly free hand. They may award to whomever they please, in whatever quantities they please, and at whatever prices they please. That of itself one would think, where there was no personal liability, and where the moneys to meet the required payments were not coming out of the bank accounts of the parties concerned, but out of the public treasury, would be sufficient to encourage an .all but unlimited degree of extravagance. But what is to be expected where, in addition to this opportunity of helping one's friends, an undertaking is given by the ministry that, no matter what the transaction, notwithstanding it is out of the taxes of the people that payments have ultimately to ibe made, the people's representatives in Parliament shall be denied all right of inquiry, all right of information, on the score that such right and knowledge are not in the public interest? And yet, Mr. Speaker, that is exactly the situation as it has existed for the past couple of years, and as it exists to-day. Is it any wonder there are huge expenditures and colossal deficits? The wonder of wonders would be how deficits could be avoided under such a system.

And the right hon. the Prime Minister stands up in this Parliament and defends that kind of thing. Well, Mr. Speaker, as long as my hon. friends opposite have that conception of public morality I see no hope of economy in public expenditures or that the taxes upon the people will be made less burdensome.
Now, Sir, in order to conceal these methods of doing business, in order to remove their possibilities from the arena of public discussion, to divert public attention and the public mind from any careful consideration of this stupendous situation, the one really menacing factor in our national life, the right hon. the Prime Minister is at great pains, whenever he speaks, whether on the platform or in this chamber, to misrepresent the position and the attitude of his opponents on the tariff, in the hope that their time will be spent in refuting his misleading statements. It is perhaps natural that he should adopt such a course. I regret that the Prime Minister is not in his seat this evening, and that he has not been in the chamber all afternoon; I should have preferred to address these remarks through you, Mr. Speaker, direct to him. However, he will, no doubt, have an opportunity of reading them, and I trust that he will pay particular attention to what I have to say in regard to the tariff. Having misrepresented, session after session, the intention of the Government itself with respect to tariff revision, it is not surprising that he should adopt the same tactics in dealing with the intention of his opponents. In the few remaining minutes that I desire to speak, may I attempt to show the nature of these misrepresentations, and at the same time restate the Liberal position as it is and as it is set forth in the amendment which is before the House? Hon members will recall that my right hon. friend, m his speech of a day or two ago, said he wished primarily to deal with the amendment. I shall endeavour to follow him in this particular, though in others I hope I may escape the ill effects of his bad example.
My right hon. friend has misrepresented the position of his opponents in three important essentials. My hon. friend, the leader of the Agrarian group (Mr. Crerar), has shown wherein this is true of himself, and hon. gentlemen with whom he is associated. May I be permitted to do the same

as respects myself and the position of the Liberal party? In this matter of the tariff, we have been misrepresented by the Prime Minister and his colleagues as to principle, as to aim, and as to method.
First, as to principle. My right hon. friend has endeavoured to have it appear that the issue, as respects the tariff, is one of free trade versus protection. Over and over again, he has made this assertion. Sometimes, oddly enough, he has said that we of the Liberal party, like himself, believed in a tariff based on the principle of protection; at other times he has said that we believe in a tariff based on the principle of free trade; then again he has said that, as respects the tariff, we have no principles, or were without any principle. Quite obviously, all three statements are not correct.. As a matter of truth, not one of them is correct. That I may do my right hon. friend no injustice, let me quote a sentence or two from one or two of his speeches. I shall give only one or two quotations, but they will have a familiar sound to hon. members of the House. Here is a quotation from a speech delivered dj the Prime Minister at Sherbroke on September 21, 1920, as reported in the Montreal Gazette of September 22. My right hon. friend said then:
What then is the issue? It is the old subject of trade policy.
Back to the old question of free trade or protection the pendulum has swung- again. Once more the people of Canada have had to decide whether one principle or the other is to prevail.
Elsewhere in the same address my right hon. friend used these words:
We have, therefore, a clear-cut issue. Do we want free trade in this country or do we not? .... The majority of the opposition to the Government of the day is composed of free traders. . . .
There is a positive statement. made by the Prime Minister of this country, although my right hon. friend knows as well as I do that the issue is not between protection and free trade. He knows that there is no free trade issue in this country at the present time.
Oh, oh.

My hon.
friend laughs. Let me repeat, Mr. Speaker, the issue is not between protection and free trade. If any one has any doubts on that score, let him read the second clause of the amendment which is before the House, and which will be supported unani-
229	.
mously, I believe, by hon. members on this side of the House. What is the first sentence of that clause? It is to the effect that existing financial requirements of the Dominion demand the maintenance of the customs tariff. So long as you recognize a customs tariff, you cannot have free trade. The tariff is, as this amendment states, a tax. It is a tax on imports, and a tax on imports is an obstruction to trade. Free trade means the absence of all tax; it means what it says, complete freedom of trade, and the raising of revenues by some other method exclusively, by income tax, for example, and when my right hon. friend says that the issue is between protection and free trade, he does not describe the situation aright. The minute a tax is imposed on trade, that moment trade is obstructed. The obstruction may be made to serve primarily one of two purposes: it may be made a means of raising revenue, or it may be made a means of affording protection to some industry within the country. Usually it serves both purposes in some measure. A tax imposed for purposes of protection will incidentally afford revenue, and a tax imposed for purposes of revenue will incidentally afford protection. The art of statesmanship in the imposition of taxation lies in making taxation as light as circumstances will permit, and in having regard for existing national needs in whatever taxation is imposed. The issue, so far as the Liberal party's attitude on the tariff is concerned, is not and never has been in this country, between free trade and protection; it has been between a tariff imposed primarily for purposes of protection, and a tariff imposed primarily for purposes of revenue.
My right hon. friend says it is either free trade or protection; that there are only the two grounds: there is no middle ground between. Let me quote his exact words:
I said a moment ago that any body of men framing a tariff must adopt one of two principles, the protective principle or the free trade principle, and I say that every public man owes it to the people to declare definitely on which of the two principles he stands.
That was a statement made at Winnipeg on October 25, 1920. The House will observe that my right hon. friend is choosing his own ground in making the alternative. He makes the assertion, and then he begins to argue from his own premises, but his premises are not right to begin with. He says:
There is a free trade tariff, and there is a protective tariff.

He goes on to say:
Is there a man or woman here who knows whether Mr. King stands for tariff on the free trade principle, or on the protection principle? You may keep on asking him, hut you will never get an answer, yes or no.
My right hon. friend knows very well that I never give an answer, "yes" or "no," on premises that are entirely false. The question is not between protection and free trade. He says, in an issue between protection and free trade, there is no middle ground. In that I agree with him, if by protection he means tariif and by free trade absence of tariff. The one is the negation of the other. That issue may be fought out theoretically, but practically there is no such issue in this country, and never has been. My right hon. friend says: "You can have two kinds of tariff and only two; you can have a tariff founded on one principle, that of protection, or another principle, that of free trade." That, Mr. Speaker, is where my right hon. friend misstates the case. You cannot have a tariff on the principle of free trade, for the principle of free trade means the absence of all tariff. What my right hon. friend should have said, what he would have said had he not deliberately been trying to becloud the issue, when speaking of the only possible alternatives of a tariff, is that there are but two kinds, a tariff based on the principle of protection, and a tariff based on the principle of revenue. Had he stated the alternative in these words, he would have correctly described the issue.
In dealing with taxation, the aim should be, as the amendment before the House states, to make taxation fall as lightly as possible upon the people of the country. The art of statesmanship as respects taxation, and as respects anything else, consists in having as much regard for the interests of the country as possible. If, when you are framing your tariff with one object or another in view, you do not take into consideration all the other objects that are to be served, you do not do your full duty to the people whose representatives you are. Unless my hon. friends opposite, when they are framing a tariff for purposes of protection, say that they will give no consideration to the revenue that is to be raised they should not hurl a stone at us because in regard to a tariff designed primarily for revenue purposes, we have some regard for the interests and needs of the country in whatever direction those needs may present themselves. As regards the tariff, my right

hon. friend has never once spoken of there being an issue between a tariff primarily for revenue and a tariff primarily for protection. He has tried to make an issue between free trade and protection, and speaking of the first alternative and omitting altogether the second, which must be as familiar to him as it is to every other hon. member of the House, he has shown that he has been trying to draw away the minds of the people from the real issue and cause them to think of something which is not the issue at all.
The position which I have just stated has been the position the Liberal party has taken in regard to the tariff since it has taken any practical interest in tariff matters. In the last speech he delivered bn the Budget before the war, the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier stated in the clearest possible terms the position of the Liberal party on the tariff. Here are Sir Wilfrid Laurier's words. They will be found in Hansard of April 23, 1914, page 2844:
We have always contended, that the policy best suited to this country is not a protective tariff hut a customs tariff for revenue purposes.
There is the statement of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. There is the statement of the Liberal party in the matter of the tariff. That is where Sir Wilfrid stood; that is where I stand; that is where our party Islands and is prepared to stand when the day of reckoning with the electorate comes.
As to the aim of our fiscal policy, my right hon. friend states that we aim to destroy the industries of Canada, though here again he finds himself in a curiously contradictory position. He says that in the West, where he alleges they want Free Trade, we are free traders, and that in the East, where he alleges they want Protection, we are protectionists. That, Mr. Speaker, would look as though, instead of seeking to destroy, we were doing our utmost to conserve.
My right hon. friend, if I may be permitted to say so, in this regard has done his utmost to misrepresent me personally, from one end of the country to the other. The other day, from his seat in the House, he could hardly wait until he had hurled across the floor at me that I particularly was being subjected to the criticism by the public that I stood in one place for one thing and *in another for another; that I particularly had created throughout the country the impression that I was trying to be all things to all men. Here is a statement of my right hon. friend as given to

the women of Toronto. I think my right hon. friend should have been a little more careful of the truth in talking to the ladies. This is from a report in the Ottawa Citizen of April 18 of a speech delivered by the Prime Minister at a meeting of the Women's Liberal-Conservative Association at Toronto on April 16:
Touching on the tariff question, Premier Meighen said that in Eastern Canada the opposition had advocated moderate protection,' and in Western Canada free trade.
Then as reported in the Mail and Empire's account of the same meeting:
In Eastern Canada, the Opposition had advocated moderate protection, and in Western Canada, free trade. Everythihg their leaders had spoken had hound them to free trade.
I should like to say to the Prime Minister of this country-I do not know whether the rules of the House will permit it-but if the rules permit it I would say that he knew that was not true when he said it. If the rules of the House so permit, I will say that, but if they do not, I will not, Mr. Speaker.

But is there any one knows where the Hon.
William Lyon Mackenzie King stands?	
Mr. King was an advocate of ruthless tariff reduction out West, but in the East he stood for the adequate protection of industry.
I challenge the right hon. the Prime M'n-ister to point to any utterance of mine in the West than can possibly be understood as meaning that I stood for ruthless tariff reduction. It is very easy to misrepresent, but it is another thing to undo the evils of misrepresentation. My right hon. friend has gone out of his way to have it appear that my attitude on the tariff has been one thing in one place and another in another. He says I have not been frank on the tariff issue. His example in that particular has been followed by his colleagues and many of his supporters, and has been
enlarged upon, of course, by his party press. Indeed, the order has gone out from my right hon. friend's office, through his publicity office, that this is to be the line of attack upon myself and the Liberal party; that it is to be made so much of a barrage on all occasions that the public is not to have an opportunity of ever learning the truth that is being obscured by this policy of misrepresentation.
As I have said, some of the colleagues of my right hen. friend the Prime Minister have followed his tactics. I was somewhat surprised to find my hon. friend the Minister of Finance doing exactly the same thing. I have here a speech delivered by my hon. friend at Peterborough in which he said, as reported in the Ottawa Citizen of January 31, of this year:	[DOT]
Now Mr. King comes into West Peterborough and tells the people that if the Liberals got into power tomorrow they would not make a single change in the tariff without first submitting it to the people.
Now that was not wholly true to begin with. I was referring to the by-election and the consequence of it, and I told the electors of Peterborough, what was true, that if on a vote of want of confidence in this House the Government opposite should be defeated, and we on this side of the House should be called upon to associate ourselves together in a Government, we would not do what hon. gentlemen opposite were then proposing to do, namely, revise the tariff, before there had been an appeal to the people, but that we would state to the people what our tariff policies and principles were, and that the people would be given a chance at a general election to pass upon them.

speechtext: That is what was said.

If that is
now my hon. friend's interpretation, I am glad to have it But what about this? My hon. friend went on to say, and this is in quotation marks :
"Out on the prairies, Mr. King is one of the most marvellous free traders and tariff-smashers you could find anywhere."
Again, I ask my hon. friend to point to a single utterance of mine which justifies that remark. He cannot do it.

I challenge
my hon. friend to bring into this House

and read to hon. members any bona fide report of any utterance of mine that justifies a statement of . that kind. Such statements, Mr. Speaker, I say are absolutely false and untrue. The speeches I made through the Canadian West were made in the hearing of thousands of persons; they were reported very fully in the western papers,' and in despatches to the East; they were made within the hearing of several hon. members of this House, and I challenge both my hon. friends, or either of them, to point to a single sentence in all that I have said which will afford a shadow of justification for their allegations. I have looked through the press reports of the different speeches I made in the different cities, and I find that every one. of them on this question of the tariff tallies, verbatim et literatim, with the policy of the Liberal party as I have already stated it in this House, and as it is known to the country. There is not a single item in any of those newspaper reports to justify any such statement as was made either by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance or the right hon. the Prime Minister.

to the House. My hon. friend knows that secret communications are not a desirable way of carrying on public business. That there may be no misunderstanding as to the position I took on the tariff during the western trip last fall, that there may be no misunderstanding as to the position I took on the tariff when I spoke in the Maritime Provinces a little over a year ago, that there may be no misunderstanding of my present attitude on the tariff may I read to the House from the account of a speech which I delivered in the city of [DOT] Toronto on August 14, of last year, before starting for the West, and which appears under the conspicuous heading, "Mr. King on All-Important Tariff Issue -A tariff for consumers and producers", on the front page of the Toronto Globe of August 16. That statement, to all intents and purposes, is identical with the presentation of the Liberal attitude on the tariff as made at every meeting at which I have spoken on the tariff since the Liberal Convention of August, 1919. It is in all essential particulars true to the Liberal platform as laid down at that convention, and it is absolutely in accord with the aim of the Liberal party on fiscal policy as set forth in the amendment before the House.

I	challenge any man or woman in this country to show that I have anywhere, at any time, swerved from the views and opinions and statement of policy a's set forth in this quotation, which is both clear and comprehensive. Before giving the quotation from the Globe-may I say this to my hon. friend from Centre Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) who I understand is to follow me, and with whom I see the Minister oi Finance is at the moment conferring, that my hon. friend from Centre Vancouver, when he spoke in this House in the debate on the Address, made certain quotations from western papers which I have looked into since, and I find that my hon. friend quoted only part of what I said and never finished the sentences. I ask him when he speaks in this debate tonight, if he reads any extracts of my speeches, not simply to pick out the parts that suit his purpose, but to read the entire paragraph. This is the quotation which I wish to give from the Toronto Globe of August 16, 1920:
Speaking on the all-important tariff question at the Liberal picnic Saturday, Hon. W. D. Mackenzie King, Liberal Leader, said:
"We believe that the time has come, indeed that it is already long past, when a downward revision of the tariff is necessary. In this revision we believe that there should ibe substantial reductions of the duties on the necessaries of life, in other words, on those articles which go to make up the food, the clothing, the shelter of the Canadian people; that certain specific articles required for the purposes of consumption and other articles essential to production should be placed upon the free list, and that in regard to the implements of production in the basic industries of agriculture, mining, lumbering and fishing there should also be a substantial reduction of duties. It is not a question of free trade or protection. ..."
"In revising the tariff to this end care will be taken of the position and needs of all the industries in our country, but such tariff as may be necessary in this connection will be, under Liberal policy, a tariff for consumers and producers, and not a tariff to further the interests of combines, monopolies or of any special or privileged classes. . . ."
"It is not honest to say that we can do away with the tariff. We can revise it, and that is the policy of the Liberal party. And I shall say in regard to tariff policies exactly the same in the city of Toronto as I shall say in the Western Provinces. I have not one message for the city and another message for the country-one message for the employer and another for the employee."

Just wait a minute. I do not know whether my hon. friend is the one who is responsible for getting his party to strike out that clause in regard to promoting trade between the Mother Country and the Dominions. It seems to me, from the nature of his remarks in the House, that he is acting as the special agent for those who were desirous to delete that clause from the party platform. Now, in the Maclean Magazine article of January 15, there is this additional sentence:
In this revision, we believe that the home and its needs should be a first consideration.
I want to emphasize that fact. I want to make it clear that in revising the tariff of this country we are going to consider first, foremost, and always, the needs of the homes of the people of the country. Then there is the further statement:
With the Liberal party, the main concern respecting: the tariff is not free trade or protection ; it is revenue, and the simultaneous development of industry in such manner as is likely to serve best the interests of the Canadian people. . . There will be required for purposes of revenue large sums of money which, of necessity, will have to be raised by indirect taxation through a customs tariff.
Now, I think I have perhaps said enough tc make clear the position which we, on
this side of the House, and which I myself, take in regard to the tariff and the principle on which it should be framed. The aim we seek in a revision of the tariff has been well set out in the amendment which is before the House. The Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) would have the country believe that our aim is to. destroy industries throughout the country, as though any political party would seek in any way co destroy the industries of a nation, and its consequent prosperity. What we aim at is well set out in these two clauses of the amendment:
That the aim of the fiscal policy of Canada should be the encouragement of industries based on the natural resource's of the country, the development of which may reasonably be expected to create healthy enterprises giving promise of enduring success:
4.	That such changes should be made in the customs duties as may be expected to reduce the cost of living, and to reduce also the cost of implements of production required for the efficient development of the natural resources of the Dominion.
That aim, I contend, is in
9	p.m. accordance with the needs of Government, in accordance with the needs of the country, and in accordance with the needs of the great body of consumers in this Dominion.
Now, finally, a word as to the method by which, if entrusted with the duty of tariff revision, we should wish to proceed. My right hon. friend the leader of the Government, when on the public hustings, has a way of describing those who disagree with him in any particular as Bolshevists, nation wreckers, I.W.Ws., O.B.JJs., and by any other epithet that denotes destruction and revolution. The right hon. gentlemen should be somewhat more careful of the language he uses. Let me say that the only aim we have is to do things in an orderly and decent manner, and that aim is well set out in paragraph 5 of the amendment:
5.	That, while keeping this aim clearly in mind, the House recognizes that in any readjustment of the tariff that may take place, regard must be had to existing conditions of trade, and changes made in such a manner as will cause the least possible disturbance of business.
When the language of this amendment is used or when in speaking I say that in revising the tariff some regard should be had to the position and needs of industry, immediately my right hon. friend gets up and says that we are in exactly the same boat as he is and out for protection. Well, I know that my hon. friend is fond of monopolies, but when has he ever had the right

to a monopoly for doing things in an orderly fashion? We on this side believe, [DOT]as respects the tariff, and as respects everything else of national importance, in proceeding along evolutionary, not along revolutionary, lines, and, if the opportunity is given to us, anything that we do shall be done exactly as described in the spirit of this amendment.
Did time permit, Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer at some length to the last clause of the amendment.
Go on.

No, I will hot. With regard to the last clause of the amendment, I desire to say only a word or two. In many respects, it is its most important part. My right hon. friend said that he intended to address himself to the amendment, but I observe that; although he spoke for two hours and a naif, he omitted altogether reference to this particular clause. No doubt he felt that reference of any kind would prove embarrassing. Let me read this final clause:
fi. That the House, while recognizing that the obligations arising from the war must be met, and declaring its readiness to make all necessary provision for that purpose, regrets that the financial proposals of the Government are not made with due regard to the economy that is so urgently needed, and expressed the opinion that, before resorting to new taxation, the Government should make a subtantial reduction in the proposed expenditure.
This clause, Mr. Speaker, goes to the root of the matter. As I have said, unless we can keep down expenditures through economy and retrenchment, tariff revision will be of little service in any respect. I might repeat what has been so truly said by hon. members as to the many ways in which economy and retrenchment might be exercised with respect to the Estimates that have been presented to the House-as to how economy might be effected as regards the railways, the Merchant Marine, the foreign credits of doubtful nature, of which I have spoken, as regards the building of dry docks and piers, and as regards certain matters in respect of which the provinces are associated with the Federal Government and which might well be left for the present to the provinces alone, such for example, as questions of technical education, housing, and the making of roads; and, also, as to how economy might be effected with respect to military, naval, and police expenditures, all expenditure which we might in very large measure considerably curtail, for a while at least.

Now, Sir, with all these statements I am -in entire accord, but what I wish to say is this: With a situation such as we have, and such as we know exists, economies effected in the directions suggested mean simply the lopping off so many branches here and there while the tree itself is decayed at the heart and rotten at the roots. We must go deeper than these surface indications and deal with the vitals and crux of the situation. It will avail but little to discuss the Budget in its details when we have a super-organization of business interests controlling the Government and dictating its policies; when we have an interweaving of financial, manufacturing, distributing and selling interests with some of their more ambitious members associated with hon. members who hold their positions in the Government against the will of the people; when we have groups of special friends helped by means of loans and foreign credits such as I have already described. When you have that kind of situation, what can be accomplished in the way of small economies here and there will have very little effect indeed in meeting the real issue. What is needed most in this country to-day is t* break this selfish combination of political autocrats and industrial plutocrats which has grown and developed during the war and fastened itself like an octopus on the people of Canada. That, Mr. Speaker, is a task which is too large to be performed by this House; it is a task which the people alone can successfully undertake. We of the Opposition may do our best, but we are powerless when the Government has in its hands, and uses against us, the weapon of the closure the minute, on matters of public expenditure, we try to let in light. The only way in which that combination can be broken is to give to the people of this country their right to have a Parliament composed of their own representatives chosen in their own way. Until that right is granted we will never know what the assets or liabilities of this country are. What is the good of discussing the Budget of my hon. friend in its few details when we have this great combination at work using public funds in all directions to further the interests of a few specially favoured groups? We may make the best effort we can-we have been doing that- but we are powerless in the face of the weapons that hon. gentlemen opposite are prepared to use on behalf of the interests that are sustaining and keeping them in power. But we do ask-and ask in the

name of the people of this country-that for the sake of Canada's present condition and for the sake of her future need, the people be granted the right-the constitutional right which is theirs-of electing a Parliament of their own choosing, and of breaking without further delay a combination which is so inimical to the public weal.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Once again I must call upon hon. members to assist the deputy speaker in upholding the dignity and decorum of Parliament. I fear that several hon. members have forgotten that these deliberations are taking place in the House of Commons.

I know my hon. friend's opposite somewhat resented my reference. I had no desire to cast any reflection upon the speech which the leader of the Opposition has delivered through the country. It was eloquent, and I propose dealing with many features of it. I want to say that I have a high regard for my hon. friend's ability on the platform. I must confess however, that I have not quite as high a regard for the conclusions which he arrives at.
Now my hon. friend has spent a good deal of time this afternoon and evening in repeating his old charge that this Government is the creation of invisible, unnamed big interests. The hon. gentleman knows that that is a very useful cry, that it appeals to a certain class of the population in this or any other country-anything that is in the nature of "a big interest" presents itself in an onimous fashion before the minds of the people. Therefore my hon. friend considers it good tactics to associate this Government, and particularly the Prime Minister, with what is known as "big interests". I have two things to say
to the House in regard to that. The first is that I think it is most unfortunate for any leader of public opinion, or anyone attempting to lead public opinion, to constantly harp upon the idea that wherever you have capital associated in companies or corporations you necessarily have corruption and that which is inimical to the best interests of the community. That is not the case. This is the day of big businesses. This is the time and the period in the development of civilization when small amounts of capital are associated in larger capital organizations for the purpose of the development of business generally. It is an economic situation, and no man has a right to constantly insinuate that there is a sinister influence behind such. The second thing I desire to say is that if there Is any foundation for what my hon. friend says, if there is any ground upon which he can base his insinuation that there is "a sinister influence"-and I use his own words-then he owes it to this House, and he owes it to the country to say what is the sinister influence and who the individuals are that he has in mind. Will my hon. friend name them? Will he tell this House what ibig interests are behind this Government and directing its affairs contrary to the interest of the country at large? I might go on and ask my hon. friend to name the large interest's of the country to which he has reference, but I think that would not be fair; I do not think it would result in any good. But my hon. friend has no right at meetings in the country, or in this House, to insinuate that there is, as he says, "a sinister" influence behind the Government in the form of "big interests".
Now I am going to deal with some matters that my hon. friend brought up. For instance the hon. gentleman spent considerable time on the system of national railway control in this country. Resort is made to tariffs, or import duties, partly to secure revenue, partly to affect the course of industry within a country. Strictly speaking, these two objects are inconsistent with each other; since a customs duty, in so far as it causes a domestic industry rather than a foreign industry to supply the market, ceases to be a source of revenue-

Where tariff duties are imposed solely for revenue, an equivalent excise tax is imposed within the country, so as to put the domestic producer precisely on the footing of his foreign competitors; and tariffs so maintained are in complete conformity with the principles of free trade.
The reason I read this definition is for the purpose of showing to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the House that we on this side stand for a tariff which has for its underlying basic principle the protection of home industries. only, you put on a moderate duty, but you put on precisely the same excise duty on the same goods manufactured within the country. I have detained the House much longer than I have intended, but interruptions have made it necessary for me to continue a short while longer.
The Government proposals in this Budget are very simple. Certain increases are proposed in internal taxation. My hon. friends opposite say that this bears heavily on the poor man. If they would examine these proposals, they would find that the heaviest increase is in the tax on spirits. Now I do not know that any one is worrying about the poor man's spirits; I do not think the poor man is himself. Food is exempt very largely, with the exception of package food. We expect to get our revenue from customs, excise, post office, and from other sources. My hon. friends directly opposite and my hon. friends angularly opposite have proposed to cut off a very serious amount of the customs tariff, and they offer to this House absolutely nothing in the place thereof. We stand on a clear-cut definite policy of a tariff of moderate protection, to the extent that is necessary to maintain the industries in Canada in a state of prosperity. That is a simple clear proposition; that is where we stand, and where we propose to stand. My hon. friends opposite talk about direct taxation, but in all the years they have been there they have not offered one single proposal of a new internal or excise tax except one and that is a tax on the unimproved value of land. I must take a moment to speak on that.
My hon. friend the leader of the Agrarian party proposed it again the other day. What does he mean by a tax on the unimproved value of land? He did not explain the tax the other day; he skated all round it, but did not explain it. According to his platform, which I have here, it means a tax on land in Canada with improvement exempt. If you have a tax of that kind, the farmers of this country will pay a very large portion of it-and perhaps that would be as well. My hon. friend

gave an illustration of what he means by a tax on land, and I saw at once what he was driving at. He was trying to show the farmers of the West that if he and his friends came into office he would put the tax on the cities. His illustration was this: There are two lots owned by one man. The man builds an apartment house on one lot, while the other lot is vacant. He said that by the building of that apartment house you increased the value of the vacant lot, and what we mean to tax, he said, is the increased value of that vacant lot. Now that is taxing the unearned increment, and not the unimproved value of the land. My hon. friend is mixed in his definitions in these various matters that he undertakes to explain with such profound authority. I repeat, that is taxing the unearned increment, and not taxing in any sense the unimproved value of the land. My hon. friend will probably say:	We intend to
tax the unimproved wild lands. How much does he expect to get from taxing the wild lands in 'Canada? It is a joke. The estimate of the best actuaries in Canada is that a 1 per cent tax on all the lands in Canada, exclusive of improvements- and that is their proposal-would bring in $80,000,000. Who would stand for a tax on all the lands in Canada? The first people would be the hon. gentleman's own followers. How many cities in Canada can stand an additional tax on land? We' tried a tax on unimproved land in Vancouver; that is, we exempted all improvements; it pretty nearly ruined the exchequer of the city of Vancouver, and we had to go back to a tax on improvements. The same thing has been tried in Alberta. Those who have tried it anywhere know the fallacy of the whole suggestion. In any case we have the municipal and provincial authorities, and this is a field of taxation which is exclusively theirs, perhaps not constitutionally, but certainly by practice. When my hon. friend seeks to pull the wool over the eyes of his followers on the prairies, he and they will have a sad awakening if the day comes when my hon. friends angularly opposite will be responsible for putting that tax in operation.
I want to make one further reference, and it is to a matter altogether apart from these debatable and controversial subjects. I refer to the appointment of a Canadian representative at Washington. I confess to the House that my mind perhaps was not so nimble as that of the hon. member
for Durham (Mr. Rowell), nor was I so well informed in international affairs as the right hon. member for King's (Sir Robert Borden), both of whom have so ably put this matter before the House. After thinking the matter over carefully, I have come to the conclusion that the Government should not delay longer in appointing a Canadian representative at Washington, and I will tell the House why. The matter is of supreme importance, and I think that I should not lose this opportunity of making a reference to it. My reason for desiring this appointment to be made without delay is that there never was a time in the history of the world when things were in such a precarious condition as they are in today. The League of Nations has been formed, it is true, and I think we all hope that the League of Nations may prosper, but we all recognize the difficulties of diverse nations, races, views, and interests, getting together in the form of a League of Nations. I think we all will agree on this also, that the commonwealth of the British Empire, this group of autonomous nations within one Empire, together with the great republic to the south, would form a magnificent foundation for a permanent league of nations. While there are those who are. endeavouring to cause division and differences between the Mother Land and the United States, I think Canada is peculiarly fitted geographically and by the genius of her people to bring together the Mother Land and the United States. Some hon. gentlemen may say:	Let us do it by
friendly commercial treaty or commercial arrangement. I say that the people of the United States are not concerned so much about our fiscal policy, any more than we are particularly concerned about theirs, except in a general way. What they are really concerned about, and what we are really concerned about, is the soul of the people, what we think of each, other, and we know this:	In all our aspirations and
ambitions the United States and Canada think very, very closely alike, and we can interpret, I think, in a manner that no other nation can the views of the United States to the Mother Land and the views; of the Mother Land to the United States. So I say to the Government, in conclusion, that in my judgment, they should hasten to fill this post at Washington so that Canada may fulfil the high destiny to which she is called.
The hon. gentleman who has just resumed

his seat (Mr. Stevens), has re-affirmed his belief in protection as the correct fiscal policy for this country. My hon. friend will absolve me from the slightest intention of giving any offence if I say that the speech which he has made to-night will not change a single vote in this House; but, Mr. Speaker, that statement could not, with the same truth, be made with reference to the possible effect of the hon. gentleman's speech outside this House. And I will tell you why. A few months ago th^ hon. gentleman had charge of the Government campaign in the then Tory riding of West Peterborough. At different points in that riding the hon. gentleman made protectionist speeches precisely similar to the one to which you have just listened. And, Sir, what was the result? The people went forth from his meetings, there and then they left the ranks of the Tory party, they ranged themselves in solid array against the Tory candidate, and on election day they declared, by an overwhelming majority of their votes, that they did not believe in the fiscal doctrines preached by the hon. member for Vancouver and that they desired to be represented in this House, not by the Tory candidate, but by the hon. gentleman who now sits here as the Liberal member for West Peterborough (Mr. Gordon). In view of that result, Sir, you will understand that it may be regarded as not improbable that the speech delivered by the hon. gentleman to-night in this House will have an effect outside of this House the very reverse of that which it may produce here, but, one that will be exactly in line with the result of his speeches in the riding of West Peterborough.
Now, the hon. gentleman, in the course of his remarks, paid a good deal of attention to the speech delivered by my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) this afternoon, a speech, Mr. Speaker, which in point of vigour, logic, and comprehensive grasp of present conditions in Canada, has not, I venture to say without fear of contradiction, been surpassed in this debate. The member for Vancouver was very wrathy at my hon. leader for having dared to say that this Government is the child of the invisible power known as the big interests. Then he went on to challenge my hon. leader to name those interests. Well, if my hon. leader means the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, and if my hon. friend from Vancouver also means the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, then, 
Sir, before I resume my seat, I shall have proved that this Government is beyond question the creature of that organization, and I will defy any hon. gentleman on the other side of the House to gainsay the fact.
Then the hon. gentleman dealt with the leader of the Opposition's criticism of the railways owned by the Government, and of the personnel and the operations of the Government Board of Railway Directors. In that connection, the hon. gentleman said that there was no objection to bringing down in this House the fullest possible information with reference to the railways and to the Board of Directors. Well, Mr. Speaker, if your memory does not altogether fail you, that must have struck you as a very strange observation, coming from the hon. member in view of the fact that it is only a few weeks ago since a resolution moved from this side of the House, asking for just that kind of information, was voted down by hon. gentlemen opposite, including the member for Vancouver himself.
The hon. member also discussed what the leader of the Opposition had said with reference to the loans made to Roumania and Greece, and he waxed eloquent on that point. Pie declared that the contracts were not let by this Government, but were let in Paris. My hon. friend, if he desired to carry complete conviction to the members of the House, and to the public outside the House, did not go far enough. Possibly-possibly, I say, Mr. Speaker,- the contracts were let in Paris; but if my hon. friend desired the hon. gentlemen sitting on this side to believe that no gentleman interested in this Government, or very close to the members of the Cabinet, had anything to do with the letting of those contracts in Paris, then he should have gone on and told the House where a gentleman named Sifton-Sir Clifford Sifton- was, about the time these contracts were being let. He should also have gone on and informed the members of the House where a few other eminent Canadian captains of industry were about the same time. Had he done that, Mr. Speaker, he would have given to the House complete and unanswerable proof of the correctness of the statements made this afternoon by the leader of the Opposition.
My hon. friend echoed a complaint upon which those who are in the tadpole stage of politics have been very eloquent during recent months. My hon, friend, .if course, has long since emerged from that

stage. He complained that the leader of the Opposition had not moved his tariff platform, because he was afraid to put the party on record with reference to that platform. Mr. Speaker, how often is it necessary for us to go on record with reference to that platform? This party,-if it is to us on this side of the House that the hon. member was referring-were members of the convention that made and adopted that platform. This party voted for that platform. So that these statements made by hon. gentlemen opposite and by their friends throughout the country consist of the merest nonsense. This platform, after having been formally adopted at the great National
11	p.m. Liberal convention, by representatives of the whole Liberal party of the Dominion of Canada, is not, Sir, to be submitted to the House unless it were intended to trifle with the House and to waste its time. This platform is intended to be submitted to the whole people of Canada at the next general election, and when it is thus submitted to the entire electorate of the country, we on this side of the House have no doubt of the overwhelming majority of the people approving that platform. Then my hon. friend went on to censure the leader of the Opposition because of criticism offered by that hon. gentleman in regard to the Government's failure to bring down a measure of tariff reform. The hon. member for Vancouver said-and I took down his words-that it was "asinine to bring down a tariff measure now." Well, the only comment that I need make upon that, Mr. Speaker, is that, adopting the language of my hon. friend, the Government were asinine in saying in the speech from the Throne that they were going to bring down a measure of tariff reform. The language is not mine. The language is that of my hon. friend and I thank him for it. Applied to the Government it is most appropriate.
Then my hon. friend took up a statement made by the leader of the Opposition that the people should govern, and with a display of what he seemed to regard as cleverness he asked who rejected reciprocity? The answer, of course, is, the people rejected it. But, Sir, may I call the hon. gentlemen's attention to the fact that the party of which he is a member, and which he so consistently supports, have paid little or no attention to the will of the people as expressed with reference to that measure, because they have taken good care to grant piece-meal what our party proposed to grant at one time by a single piece of legislation. And, Sir, in this connection, as differentiating the two parties and marking the essential and eternal difference between Liberalism and Toryism, it must be remembered that had our late distinguished leader so willed it the reciprocity measure could have been put through Parliament by the adoption of closure but he said:	No, we do not believe in coercion. We will not put this measure through by such means. We will never adopt closure while we are in power in this country. That, Sir, is a feature of the matter which should not be overlooked, and I mention it in case my hon. friend should have occasion to refer to the subject again.
Then the hon. gentleman directed his attention to my hon. friend the member for Marquette. He criticised him in rather severe terms and he challenged what my hon. friend had said with reference to the kind of canvass that is going on down in the constituency of York-Sunbury. He disputed the statement made the other day that the electors there are being asked to vote for the Government candidate on the ground that the Catholics are supporting the farmer candidate. In support of the denial of that statement by the Prime Minister the hon. gentleman read a telegram from the Tory candidate in the county of York-Sunbury. On that aspect of the dispute I do not wish to make any further observation. But the hon. gentleman also challenged the statement of the hon. member for Marquette with reference to an offer having been made to the Hon. P. J. Veniot, the Catholic representative in the Government of New Brunswick, to become a member of this Cabinet. The hon. gentleman laid much stress on the fact that the Prime Minister had categorically denied that statement, and he evoked the cheers of those around him by denouncing the hon. member for Marquette for having made it. Well, Sir, it happens that at this moment I am in a position to settle the dispute upon that point; and if I make no other contribution to the debate than the one that I am just about to make, then in all modesty I may aver that I will have rendered a public service to this country at the present time. The hon. member cited the denial of his leader that any offer had been made to the Hon. P. J. Veniot to become a member of this Government. Well, Sir, it so happens that the Canadian Press despatches to-day carry an article giving an interview with Mr. COMMONS
Veniot, the man whom the hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House will admit is the man best qualified to tell what did take place with reference to the question under discussion. This is the article:
St. John, N.B., May, 19.
In reference to the claim of Hon. T. A. Crerar, leader of the Progressive in the House of Commons last Tuesday that Premier Meighen or his agents had approached "the Catholic Minister of Public Works in New Brunswick Hon. (P. J. Veniot), with a view to his coming into the Government," and Mr. Meighen's denial that any such offer had been made by him, or w-ith his authority, Mr. Veniot is quoted in a special despatch to-day as stating:
"I would have preferred, not to have discussed this matter, but in view of Premier Meighen's statement and the attempt made by the Conservative press to leave the impression that I sought the position instead of the position me, I feel, in justice to myself and my friends, I should break the silence maintained by me since first I was approached in December last with the request that I consider an offer to enter the Meighen Cabinet."
"Let me first say that I had no part in giving information on which certain questions asked in the House of Commons were based. I never authorized the use of my name in this connection."
"In view of all that has taken place in connection with this matter, I am, to say the least, surprised at the statement reported to have been made by the Prime Minister in the House on Tuesday last, when he left the impression that he knew absolutely nothing about any overtures made to me."
"The person who made the overtures to me presented to me a letter addressed to him and signed by Premier Meighen.
This letter showed that the Premier was in close touch with the situation, and, further, I may say that a certain other Cabinet Minister also wrote to this same person. It is scarcely necessary to add that the party who made the overtures is a strong and influential Conservative."
"I never sought the position, and my reply, dated January 11, 1921, can be produced to prove this when the proper time arrives. Should I ever aspire to fundamental"-
Evidently the word "fundamental" is a mistake.
-"honours, I would not attempt to obtain such honours, by a base betrayal of my Liberal principles and the friends with whom I have been politically associated during the last thirty-five years. I still have faith in the grand old Liberal Party, and that faith cannot be shaken by any offers made by Premier Meighen and his friends."

May I ask
my hon. friend a question? My hon. friend has read a letter of which I did not hear the whole, but the purport of which, if I understand it, is that Premier Meighen authorized some one to approach the gentleman who is referred to with an offer of a position in the Cabinet. Is that the purport of the letter?
Read it again.

I have no objection to
my hon. friend asking a question, but in reply to his question I just want to say that I prefer not to be interrupted in my speech, and that this despatch-
Oh, oh.

I want to see who is
laughing, because I can change that laugh in half a minute.

It will be changed
pretty soon.

"The loud laugh
denotes the vacant mind."

The despatch I have
read tells exactly what was done in the language of Mr. Veniot and my hon. friend can see it for himself. Now on this point this document, Mr. Speaker-

I have read the
