No, I do not refuse to read Mr. Veniot's interview in the right hon. gentleman's hearing. That is not my reason for refusing to read it again. I have already read it, and the right hon gentleman should have been in his place to hear it.
In the course of this debate there have been various references to the right hon. gentleman's speech delivered a few days ago in this House. It was not my privilege to hear the right hon. gentleman, so I have been obliged to form my opinion of his speech by reading it, by hearing opin ions expressed about it, and by listening to a discussion of it here in the House. This afternoon my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition stated that in his opinion the lengthy speech of the right hon. gentleman in its duration of two and one-half hours did not contain a single human note. My impression is, Sir, that that is a correct

description of the speech. It might have been an appropriate speech for the right hon. gentleman to deliver a few years ago when he was the chief slugger of the Borden Administration, but I submit it was not the kind of speech that we have a right to expect from the Prime Minister of Canada. I say, further, Sir, that there was neither dignity nor leadership in the speech, and that it was remarkable mostly for-
Slugging.

-for what it omitted rather than for what it contained. The right hon. gentleman devoted almost his entire time to an attack on members of the Opposition; but he had nothing to say about the question of unemployment or the remedy for it; he had nothing to say about the high cost of living or a measure of relief to reduce it; he had nothing to say about curbing public expenditures; nor had he anything to say about any policy to increase Canada's fexport trade.
Possibly, Sir, we have the key to the last omission in a report that appeared in this morning's Citizen, giving the substance of a speech delivered at Toronto 'last evening by Mr. Lloyd Harris, a friend of this Government and a gentleman who has occupied a very prominent place in the business life of this country. The despatch is as follows:
Toronto, May 18th, Lloyd Harris, former Canadian Trade Commissioner, addressing the Canadian Confectionery, Biscuit and Chocolate Manufacturers at a banquet tonight which concluded the annual convention of the organization, said: "Canada's export trade in Great Britain was suffering because of our present political system. The Government is so inefficient," he said, "that it has less business understanding than a boy in the street."
And strangely enough, Sir, on the very day that the report of that speech appears there is given ocular demonstration to the members of this House and to visitors in the gallery that this business inefficiency even extends to the length of its being impossible for the Government to put two clocks on the walls of this chamber that will both tell the same time! As you will observe one is 10 minutes ahead of the other. And on the point of Government inefficiency it may also be observed that while my hon. friend from Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) did not specifically mention it, it may be assumed that he had Mr. Lloyd Harris' words in his mind when he strongly urged the Government to disregard the opinions of the hon. member for Durham
(Mr. Rowell) and the right hon. member for King's, N.S. (Sir Robert Borden), and to hurry up and appoint a trade commissioner at Washington.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it is not improbable that my opinion of the Budget, which has been more or less under discussion in this House for the past ten days, might be conjectured with a fair degree of accuracy, even if I refrained from giving expression to my views on the subject. However that may be, I deem it a duty that I owe to Parliament, to my constituents and to the country at large that I should state briefly and plainly what my position is, and at the same time make known the reasons for the vote that I intend to give upon the amendment that has been moved by my colleague the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding).
To the merest tyro in politics it is as clear as the noonday sun that this Budget was born of the necessities of the Government. In the Speech from the Throne at the opening of the session, as has been frequently said, a revision of the tariff was promised, but now when the Budget is brought down near the end of the session it does not contain the promised revision, and we are told that there will not be any revision of the tariff for some time to come. In other words, the Budget is the makeshift product of a makeshift government. For that very reason it has given fresh stimulus to the commercial unrest that a comprehensive and stable policy would be a prime factor in removing. Already merchants are protesting against some of its features that, in their application, are held to be injurious to the normal and proper conduct of business, and it is certain that as time passes this feeling will increase in intensity, just as the feeling against the luxury tax did, so that nobody need be surprised to see the Minister of Finance again recede from his position as he did on a former occasion. There can be no doubt, Sir, that, like the policeman in Gilbert and Sullivan's opera, the Finance Minister's lot "is not a happy one." Indeed, on this side of the House we should be disposed to extend greater sympathy to him if he had not given us such abundant proof that he is mentally constituted like the great majority of children, some women, and a considerable number of men, who do not realize the danger of certain tasks that they attempt.
Opposition members have sought to impress upon the Minister of Finance, the futility of trying to re-establish equili-

brium in our national business affairs by piling taxes upon taxes while useless expenditure goes on unchecked.
On that point I want to add a word.
It is true that the Minister of Finance and some of his colleagues in the Government preach economy, but, Sir, it is truer still that they do not practise economy. There has been a carnival of unnecessary expenditure in connection with the railways, the merchant marine, the militia, and the transfer of the mounted police froni their natural and useful field of action in the West to an unnatural and an indefensibly expensive field of inaction in the East. Added tto all this there have been new and 'hitherto unheard of schemes invented to spend public moneys, such as the housing scheme and the jobs created for and the financial rewards given to, scores upon scores of so-called Liberals who deserted their party in 1917. The net result is that no matter what amount may be raised by taxation, a large portion of it is put to uses from Which the public as a whole derives no benefit whatever.
Dealing with this subject, the Toronto Globe in an editorial published a few months ago said:
At a time when Britain has been cancelling debt at the rate of almost a hundred million dollars a month Canada is barely holding the net debt down to the figures shown at the completion of demobilization. The need for thrift in the various departments of the national service was never more urgent than it is to-day. There is no justification for the spending of public money at the rate of over $360,000,000 a year, even though that vast sum includes interest and sinking fund on the national debt. The Canadian people cannot stand taxation of almost $40 per year for every man, woman and child in the country. The load is intolerably great.
In view of the official figures, Sir, that have been made public since the editorial from which I have just quoted was written, the statement of the Globe has even greater weight to-day than it had when it was published a few months ago. But having regard to the forces behind this Government, it is, I fear, too much to expect that they will practice economy even if they desired to do so.
As a contrast, Mr. Speaker, with what has been their practice I am reminded of an incident that was told me to illustrate the spirit of thrift that animated Mr. Gladstone, the greatest of British statesmen.
A few* years ago Mr. Lloyd George was showing me over the premises in Downing Street which he then occupied as Chancellor of the Exchequer. He directed my attention to a small plot of bare ground,

possibly about fifty feet square, forming part of the government property immediately in the rear of his official residence. With a smile, he told me that Mr. Gladstone when Chancellor of the Exchequer had occasion to point out the same plot of ground to a friend and that the friend had suggested that it should be graded and sodded. Mr. Gladstone instantly turned and said: Sir, where is the money to come from? Merely to recall the incident, Mr. Speaker, is to illustrate, without any comment of mine, how sadly Mr. Gladstone would be out of place as a member of the present Government of Canada.
Hon. gentlemen who have preceded me on this side of the House have discussed the Government's Budget and its tax proposals in such detail that at this stage of the debate I do not think that anything could profitably be added to what they have said if I were to discuss any special features of the Government's policy. I will, therefore, confine my observations to a brief review of the tariff position taken by some hon. gentlemen opposite and then to an exposure of a few of the methods adopted by protectionists to attain their chief object is life, namely the fleecing of the Canadian public.
The hon. Minister of Militia and Defence (Mr. Guthrie) who, I hope, is in the chamber at .the moment, in his several tariff speeches during the present session paid a good deal of attention to the Opposition, and their attitude towards the tariff seemed to disturb my hon. friend. Well, Sir, as I listened to the hon. gentleman the thought occurred to me that what was really troubling him was not the present tariff attitude of the Opposition but the ghosts of some of his own former speeches on the tariff. In times past,. Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman took a very different attitude with regard to the tariff from that which he has recently taken in this House. I do not propose to go over all the tariff pronouncements made by my hon. friend, but, with perfect fairness to him I can indicate by a few references just where he stood upon the tariff a very short time ago and what he thought about the Government that then advocated a brand of protection similar to that which is advocated by the Government of which he is now a member.
When the Bill introduced by the Borden Government for the purpose of creating a tariff commission was under discussion in this House in February, 1912, the hon. gentleman took very strong exception to it.

After having described the Bill as "nothing more nor less than a cheap Yankee device of the Finance Minister copied from the United States, a device notoriously invented hy the high protectionist party in the United States," and having further alleged that the Bill was " intended to sustain the glorious doctrine of protection," the hon. gentleman let in the light on his present political associates in a few biting sentences. They may be found on page 2604 of Hansard of 1912. They were as follows:
This Bill cannot be said to be original in any respect. There are only two or three countries,
I believe, in the world-only two or three at all events, of which I know-which have adopted tariff commissions and it is a strange thing that the countries which have adopted this method of procedure are the highest protected countries in the world. A tariff commission board seems to be a necessary adjunct to the high protective system, and I do not think I am going one jot beyond the truth when X say that this Bill is brought in here-almost the first important Bill of the the first session of this Parliament-as a quid pro quo for the Canadian manufacturers'. Association to redeem the promises made to them for their generous and lavish support during the election on the 21st day of September last.
Having thus exposed how his present bedfellows proposed to reward their benefactors, the hon. gentleman declared that "the farmers of Ontario are .not high protectionists," and then, having stated his own position in these words: "A tariff for revenue affords enough protection in my community and, in my opinion, it is sufficient"-the hon. gentleman wound up his excellent speech by moving that the Bill be given the six months' hoist.
Now Sir, the position taken on the occasion to which I have just referred by the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence was a fairly advanced position, but he made still greater progress toward freedom of trade during the following twelve months.
It will he remembered that there was a by-election in the constituency of South Bruce in the month of October, 1913. The hon. gentleman took part in that byelection and he delivered a number of stirring speeches in behalf of the successful Liberal candidate, the hon. member who at present represents South Bruce (Mr. Truax) in this chamber. One of the meetings that was addressed hy the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence was held at Walkerton on October 23, 1913. At that meeting a speech was delivered in support of the Tory candidate by the present right hon. Prime Minister. It fell to the lot of my hon. friend, who is now a
colleague of the Prime Minister, to reply to the latter on that occasion, and from the report of his speech published in the Toronto Globe on October 24, 1913, I take the following paragraphs:
Kvery day since the present Government assumed office the cost of living had been increasing. Prices were being held up by the trusts and combines. There was a call in the country for a Government that was strong enough to break the flour combine, the canners' combine and the packers' combine.
We want a Government that is strong enough to go to these people and say that the cost of living must be reduced. I will stand up in the House of Commons, or :n the country, for free food for the people of Canada. Where was Mr. Meighen, too. on the duty on agricultural implements? He had moved a resolution in the House of Commons to have the duty on farming machinery reduced, but now that he was in the Government nothing was heard of it.
I call upon the Minister of Militia and Defence (Mr. Guthrie) to redeem the public promise that he made in the riding of South Bruce in the year 1913. I call upon him to stand up in this House and demand free food for the people of Canada. If he does not do so then out of his own, mouth will he stand condemned; and hy that broken pledge rather than hy any mandate from the people, will he justify his continuing to hold a portfolio in this Cabinet of broken pledges.
During the past year the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne) has made a number of speeches on the tariff in the country and in Parliament. His most recent speech on this subject was made in this debate a few days ago. In all his speeches the hon. gentleman has assumed a critical attitude towards the Liberal party and, stated in general terms, his position has been that he supported the tariff policy of Sir Wilfrid Laurier; that the Liberal party has abandoned that policy and substituted another which is not the one which Sir Wilfrid advocated, and that in consequence, the hon. gentleman cannot support the Liberal party. Now, Sir, let us examine these assertions.
Granting that the hon. gentleman supported the Liberal tariff policy down to the year 1911, I contend that his support of that policy ceased in that year. Recently I had occasion to read a list of names of certain Liberals in Montreal who opposed their party on the reciprocity issue in 1911. Included in the list there is a gentleman named Ballantyne, and upon making inquiry I was told by Montreal friends that the gentleman who is thus designated and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries are one and the same person. That being so, it is evident that the hon. gentleman

broke with his party on the tariff issue in 1911 and that on fiscal matters he was not, from that time on, a follower of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. Therefore, I cannot admit the claim set up by the hon. gentleman, based on the incorrect statement, that he was a consistent follower of Sir Wilfrid's tariff policy.
Now let us examine the other branch of his statement that the present tariff policy of the Liberal party is not the policy of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and that it is a substitute for the one advocated by the late leader of the Liberal party.
In the House of Commons on May 23, 1917, the Hon. Frank Oliver moved, and Mr. F. B. Carvell, then member for Carleton, N.B., seconded this resolution:
1.	That, wheat, wheat flour and all other products of wheat be placed upon the free list.
2.	That farm implements and machinery, farm tractors, mining-, flour and saw-mill machinery, and repa'rs for same, rough and partly dressed lumber, illuminating, lubricating and fuel oils, cement and fertilizers be added to the free list.
3.	That staple foods and food products (other than wheat flour) domestic animals- and foods therefor, be admitted into Canada free of duty when coming from and being the product of, any country admitting like Canadian articles into such country free of duty.
4.	That substantial reductions be made in the general tariff on all articles imported into Canada, excepting luxuries.
5.	That the British preference be increased to 50 per cent of the general tariff.
Upon reference to the Parliamentary records of the date mentioned, it will be found that Sir Wilfrid Laurier supported and voted for the resolution that I have just read. That resolution, therefore, embodies Sir Wilfrid's tariff policy on May 23, 1917.
Later on in the year 1917, in his election address of November of that year, Sir Wilfrid Laurier thus defined his position on the tariff:
In further mitigation of disadvantages to agricultural production, I would immediately remove the duties on agricultural implements and other essentials, as demanded by the western farmers. A general well-considered reform of the tariff for the purpose of helping Canadian production and relieving the Canadian consumer would also be an object of my administration.
These words make it plain that at the end of 1917 Sir Wilfrid stood on the same tariff platform as he had advocated earlier in that year.
The last public address delivered by Sir Wilfrid Laurier was his speech at the convention of the Eastern Ontario Liberal Association on January 14, 1919, just about a month before he died. The convention

had adopted a comprehensive tariff resolution summarizing the Liberal party's record from 1893 to 1919, and declaring for a downward tariff revision in accordance with the resolution moved by Mr. Oliver and seconded by Mr. Carvell in the House on May 23, 1917, and in expressing his approval of the action of the convention, Sir Wilfrid spoke as follows:
In the resolution which was passed upon this subject at the convention of 1893, we declared against the principle of protection, and when we had the opportunity we lived up to our declaration. Sir, it has always been made a cause of reproach to us that when in office we did not adopt but were recreant to our declarations. Such a reproach cannot reach us. We were not recreant, we proceeded step by' step towards the goal, always keeping it in view, never imposing a duty for protection's sake only, but always acting upon the principle or the basis of a tariff for revenue and revenue only. This was our policy in the past, it is our policy to-day and we have taken this occasion to reaffirm it. Sir, as I have already told you, the reproach is made to us that we were recreant to our declarations, to our policy. This reproach is well rebuked already by the declaration which you have passed this afternoon, reciting what we have done, reciting the many articles which we placed upon the free list, and reciting the many articles upon which we made a reduction of duty. But there are two features especially of our policy which will stand at all events, one will stand forever, and the other will soon be restored, I believe. The first policy which we affirmed upon succeeding to office was the policy of a British preference.
Then, after giving the details of the different stages in connection with the several increases of the British preference, Sir Wilfrid proceeded:
This was done in spite of all the opposition of the Conservative party.
And I might interrupt the reading of Sir Wilfrid Laurier's speech at this point by recalling that the hon. member for Vancouver, when he was speaking a little earlier this evening, said that, when there was any question of trading with Great Britain, that touched hon. gentlemen opposite on a tender Spot. There can not have been much tenderness in that spot when the Liberal party introduced the British preference because, as Sir Wilfrid Laurier says, we adopted it "in spite of all the opposition of the Conservative party." Sir Wilfrid continued:
And upon what ground was their objectioi based? t Simply upon the ground that we should have exacted preference for preference, that if we gave preference to the goods of Great Britain, that country should give us the preference for our goods. That was not our policy. We said: "No, we are not going to bargain with the Mother Country upon matters of that kind. We do it because we are British subjects, and because we believe in the principles of free trade. We believe

also that it is for the good of the Canadian people that we should adopt that policy, and by that policy we stand to-day also. In your resolution your affirm that the black eye which was given by the present Government three years ago should be removed, and, Sir, if it is in our power to do so, we shall do so. At all events, we shall take the opportunity to bring the matter before Parliament at the next session."
Then a little later on in the same speech Sir Wilfrid Laurier dealt with the subject of reciprocity, and he said:
Sir, there was another feature of our policy another attempt that we made at freer trade- this time not with Great Britain, but with oui neighbours, the American people. .	.	. Bet
me say here that if ever there was a polioy which would have been beneficial to the Canadian people, it was the agreement which was made between iMr. Fielding and the Government of IMr. Taft.
However, that policy was defeated. It was met with the cry, of "no truck or trade with the Yankees,'' Which was stupidity itself, and I am sorry to say they carried the country with it. But, Sir, revenge is sweet at all times, sweet even to me who profess to be a good Christian. Revenge is sweet, and do you know *why? My revenge is in the attitude of the Conservative party who have proclaimed no truck or trade with the Yankees, and yet had to go to Washington, reluctantly, I admit, very reluctantly, but under the threat of the western farmers, who were asking for free wheat with the Americans, they had to go-the consequence is that to-day we have free wheat. But that is not all. They had to make another advance to the Americans, not for the farmers of the West this time, but for the farmers of the East. The growers of potatoes in Prince Edward Island and in New Brunswick made demands, and so those in power had to adopt the American offer of free potatoes; and so to-day the potatoes raised by eastern growers are free in the American market. There was still another step, and this one was taken, not by adopting the Washington legislation, but simply by action at Ottawa. They gave free tractors to the farmers of the West, this action being taken by Order in Council. I had no objection to such Order in Council. I would almost forgive them the others if they would pass more of this kind.
Now, what do these piece-meal advances in reciprocity mean? They are simply an admission that these people were acting stupidly- to pu-t it no stronger than that-when they refused the offer made by the Americans of extended free trade with them. If there ever was anything stupid in the world surely it was the action of the Conservatives in 1911, in declaring that we Canadians, numbering less than 8,000,000 of people, should refuse to trade with the wealthiest nation on earth to-day, the American people.
He concluded that branch of his address with these words:
Of course, they have the satisfaction of having won office upon the stupid anti-reciprocity cry, but better lose ten times over than triumph by such methods as that. For we know that if there is one thing which, more than any other is conducive to good relations between
nation and nation it is trade. And, though our commercial relations with our neighbours have not been as free or as friendly as I would like to have them, and though we lost a great opportunity in 1911 to make them more friendly than they were, still, thank Heaven, we have the satisfaction of knowing that for over a hundred years we have had no war with our American neighbours. That is a great triumph.
There, Sir, you have in Sir Wilfrid Laurier's own words his dying message as it were on the subject of the tariff. Now, after that, what did the Liberal party do? Did it, as the Minister of Marine and Fisheries claims, depart from the position taken by Sir Wilfrid and substitute another policy for his? It did nothing of the kind. At a great National Convention-such a convention, Mr. Speaker, by the way, as the Tories have never had the courage to hold -the Liberal party affirmed the policy which Sir Wilfrid had advocated by voice and vote, and it did so in a resolution whose terms are practically identical with those of the resolutions supported by Sir Wilfrid in 1917 and in January 1919. So that there may be no doubt on that point, I will read the resolution adopted by the National Liberal Convention in August 1919. It is as follows:
That the best interests of Canada demand that substantial reductions of the burdens of Customs taxation be made with a view to the accomplishing of two purposes of the highest importance: First: diminishing the very high cost of living which presses so severely on the masses of the people; Second: reducing the cost of the instruments of production in the industries based on the natural resources of the Dominion, the vigorous development of which is essential to the progress and prosperity of our country.
That, to these ends, wheat, wheat flour and all products of wheat; the principal articles of food: farm implements and machinery; farm tractors, mining, flour and saw-mill machinery and repair parts thereof; rough and partly dressed lumber; gasoline, illuminating, lubricating and fuel oils; nets, net-twines and fishermen's equipments; cements and fertilizers should be free from Customs duties, as well as the raw material entering into the same.
That a revision downwards of the tariff should be made whereby substantial reductions should be effected in the duties on wearing apparel and footwear, and on other articles of general .consumption (other than luxuries), as well as on the raw material entering into the manufacture of the same.
That the British preference be increased to 56 per cent of the general tariff.
And the Liberal Party hereby pledges itself to implement by legislation the provision of this resolution when returned to power.
Now if the language of that resolution be compared with the resolutions publicly supported by Sir Wilfrid Laurier in 1917 and in January 1919, it will be found that the Liberal party to-day stands exactly

where Sir Wilfrid stood up to the last hour of his life; and if my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries wants to see those who have abandoned the tariff policy of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, let him look first at the seats around him on his own side of the House, and then if he desire to complete the survey, let him look in his own mirror. Therefore, I say, let us hear no more of the silly talk that the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries indulges in when he says that he follows the tariff policy of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and that we of the Liberal party have abandoned it.
Here let me interject, Mr. Speaker, an observation based on the presence in the Liberal party's tariff platform of a declaration in favour of increasing the British preference fifty per cent. Every time that is mentioned by anybody on this side of the House, up jumps the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and asks:	Do you
mean that? I have been wondering, Sir, whether the physical agility which the mention of that phrase, British preference, imparts to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has any relation to the fact that British manufacturers are famous the world over for making a superior quality of paint?
Now should my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries act on my suggestion and make a survey of the Liberal backsliders on his side of the House, one of the first upon whom his gaze will fall will be his colleague the hon. Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder). For that reason, and for other reasons as well, this hasty sketch of party fence-jumping would be minus its most attractive feature if the Minister of Immigration and Colonization were left out of the picture. Therefore, I will devote a few minutes to the hon. gentleman before I hasten on to the concluding part of my remarks.
In July last the hon. gentleman assisted at the birth of an alleged new party, and was one of the sponsors for the name adopted, the National Liberal and Conservative party-a double linchpin name. Following that event, it was announced that my hon. friend would be one of the members of the Tariff Commission, and that he would make a tour of the country with that body. For some reason that has not yet been disclosed, the hon. gentleman did not take up bis duties with the Tariff Commission, but he did make a tour with the right hon. the Prime Minister. It was understood, Sir, at the time, that the Minister of Immigration and Colonization was to ac-

company his leader in the role of a political economist to preach sound fiscal doctrines in the West. You can therefore imagine the surprise, Mr. Speaker, of the right hon. the Prime Minister, and the vast amusement of the rest of the Dominion, when the Minister of Immigration and Colonization suddenly discarded the role of political economist and stood forth at a meeting one night in the character of an ornitholigist. declaring that in previous years, when he had spoken about the tariff, he had spoken as a parrot. Pursuing this new role, he endeavoured, but in vain, to convince his audience that he now spoke upon the tariff as an owl; and, on the authority of some of those who were present on more than one occasion, it can be asserted that the western people refused to take any more stock in the hon. gentleman as an ornithologist than they took in him as a political economist. Now, if the hon. gentleman is still pursuing his researches in ornithology, and if his analytical mind still occupies itself with a dissection of the elements of the party with which he is facing a lingering but inescapable fate, let me assist him in his studies by referring him to a few paragraphs in a speech delivered by Sir Richard Cartwright to the Young Liberal Club of Seaforth, Ontario, On October 27, 1886. These paragraphs are as follows:
I want to say a few words to you on the proper relations which should subsist between Liberals and Conservatives. I want you to understand distinctly that in my opinion there is not necessarily, and ought not to be, any conflict between true. Liberals and true Conservatives. According to my view of the situation Liberalism and Conservatism are rather the complement and supplement of each other than the necessary opposites. So to speak, I would say that Liberalism represents the masculine element, and Conservatism the feminine element in politics, all the world over. Don't let my Conservative friends here-if any such be present-for one moment suppose that with my view's of the rights and functions and future place of women, when I speak of Conservatism as the feminine principle in politics, I do anything else than pay Conservatives an extremely high compliment. . . . We must recollect that it is the duty of the stronger to respect the weaker vessel. Both are wanted in a well ordered state if you can get them of the right sort. So I say to my young friends, be Conservative or Liberal, as you please ; still I say also: Be one thing or the other. Let there be no halting between two opinions. If there be one thing I do abhor and detest, it is those Laodiceans of the commonwealth, those political mulattos who inherit the vices of both parties, and the virtues of neither; who seek to hunt with the hounds and run with the hare; who blow now hot and now cold; who, when political exigencies require it are ready to swear that black Is white, that orange is green, that a circle is square, or a square is round, who are prepared to call themselves

Cat ho li e-Protestants, or Prates tan t-Cat ho l ies, if they may thereby get a vote; whose principles are to have no principles; those men whose name is a lie in terms, which the other title of the animal is-"Liberal-Conservative." If any of that particular description of gentry object, Sir, I am willing to indulge them with another comparison. I revert to my original metaphor. If it be true, as I have intimated above, that Conservatism is the feminine and Liberalism the masculine element in politics, it follows, as a matter of course, that "Liberal-Conservative" represent the neuter gender-a barren, sterile, unfruitful generation, productive only of debts, of taxes, and of scandals.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if my hon. friend the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Calder), will bring his acute mind to bear upon the sentences I have just quoted, he will readily see that in the case of himself and his associates who are banded together under a name which, as good old Sir Richard said, "is a lie in terms," history is merely repeating itself, and the same fate awaits those who have adopted this new camouflage as the one that overtook the party that was held up to ridicule before the Young Liberals of Seaforth in 1886. For the sake of old times, let me offer a suggestion to my hon. friend. If, before the inevitable happens, the hon. gentleman should by any chance have occasion to address meetings in Western Canada again, I would suggest that he abandon ornithology and appear as a zoologist. If he will do that, and if he will then tell his audiences that, when he is speaking on the tariff, he is speaking, not as a parrot, but as a chameleon, he will make the hit of his life-
12	m. Mr. Speaker, in the Budget, as well as in the speeches supporting it, the feature that stands out most prominently is the concern of the Government to protect the interests of the few at the expense of the interests of the many. Protection is thrust forward so aggressively that new meaning is given to the phrase that "it is a condition and not a theory" that the Canadian people have to face. What the condition is may be gauged by an exposure of some of the methods that have been employed to produce it, and that are now being used in an organized effort to make it permanent in this country.
Many of the members of the House, perhaps all, will have read, occasional protests on the part of certain newspapers against the attempts of Mr. G. M. Murray, the former secretary of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, to control editorial opinion by the giving or withholding of advertisements. How that gentleman has been operating is not so well known, and as his operations are financed by the beneficiaries of protection, and are designed for the sole purpose of stifling or [DOT] corrupting public opinion for the benefit of those who enjoy protection, it is in the public interest that the character and extent of these operations be made known. In general outline, that is what I now propose to do.
For six months or more prior to his resignation as secretary of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, Mr. Murray served on a number of Government boards and commissions. In reality, his services were loaned to the Government, because he was paid throughout by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. After resigning his secretaryship in the association, Mr. Murray began to collect his staff for the business in which he is now engaged, a business, Mr. Speaker, which is without precedent in Canada. Indeed, I doubt whether any parallel for it can be found in any other country in the world.
Mr. Murray operates through a company called "Murray's Editorial Report Service," with headquarters at Toronto. The chief business of this company is to collect the views of every Canadian daily newspaper, and Mr. Murray is assisted in this work by a corps of university graduates, who are supposed to be experts in "sizing up," as it is termed, any newspaper. Reports are sent out at irregular intervals to the company's patrons, or are given to them when called for. These reports are designed to guide the company's subscribers in the placing of their contracts for advertising space, and papers that advocate protection are always given the preference.
With funds supplied chiefly by Eastern manufacturers. Mr. Murray established two other companies to extend the scope of his operations. One was "Publishers News Service Limited," at Regina, and the other was "Canadian Newspaper Service Limited" at Hamilton. The former company was to put out in the West what are known as "Datent insides" or ready prints for the newspapers, and the last named company was to perform similar work in the East. It was claimed that through these two agencies about 140 papers would be supplied with protectionist "patent insides".
The whole business under Mr. Murray's control has been conducted under a cloak of secrecy, and the names of the patrons of this unique service have not as yet been divulged. To keep up the mystery

all the subscribers to the service have been furnished with a chart or analysis of the Canadian daily newspaper field from the standpoint of the editorial policy pursued by each publication. This chart or analysis is a mass of symbols, letters, and numerals that can be translated into ordinary language only if the Key to the analysis is at hand.
Now, Sir, it will be of interest to the House, and of even greater interest to the country, to learn how the chart or analysis, as interpreted by the Key, deals with the Canadian newspapers. For an illustration let me take two of the leading Canadian dailies, namely the Toronto Mail and the Toronto Globe.
In the analysis the name of the Toronto Mail is preceded by the symbol formed by the two pairs of crossed lines used to denote the word "number." According to the Key this means that the Mail is "Unionist in politics" and "supports Meighen." Then after the name of the Toronto Mail, there are in separate columns, under appropriate headings, the following letters and numerals:
/"A.l." Which means: "Gives good comprehensive news service covering both general and local fields. Excellent,-the best."
"E.l." Which means:	"Well written
editorials, clever in argument, forceful in expression, carrying conviction."
"J.l." Which means: "Gives expression to safe and sane views on Labour, Industrial Unrest, and Socialism, denounces extremes of all kinds, pleads for moderation, etc. Discusses the subject very frequently."
"N.l." Which means: '"Supports a protective tariff with or without revision. Discusses the subject very frequently."
"R.l." Which means: "Generally sympathetic with Business",-business, Mr. Speaker, with a big B-"apparently desirous of seeing it get a square deal." "Fair in argument and truthful in statement. Discusses the subject very frequently."
"U." Which means: "Specially deserving of support. Sound on practically all points. Alert and capable in defence of Business."
Again business with a big "B." That ends the analysis of the Toronto Mail. Now let us see what is set down about the Toronto Globe.
In the analysis, the name of the Toronto Globe is preceded by the two symbols used in currency to indicate dollars and pounds. Again turning to the Key, it will be found that these mean that the Globe is "Liberal

and Farmer" in politics and that it "supports King and Crerar." After the name "Toronto Globe" there appears the following letters and numerals:
"A.l." Which gives it the same rating as the Mail for news service.
"E.l." Which means that in editorial ability the Globe is on a par with the Mail.
"H.4." Which means "shows strong editorial bias on subjects not hereinafter covered. Anti-Union Government."
"J.l." Which means: "That the Globe's views on Labour, Industrial Unrest and Socialism are the same as those of the Mail and are expressed as frequently;" "0.1." Which means: "Favors low tariff with considerable extension of free list and all-round reduction on the remainder; favors reciprocity with the United States. Discusses the subject very frequently." "T.l." Which means:	"Generally antagonistic towards Business, or given to misrepresentation and unfair arguments, or featuring the bad and saying nothing about the good. Discusses the subject very frequently."
"X." Which means:	"Unfair. Bad
points outbalance good. Objectionable." And there, Sir, the analysis leaves the Globe. Other examples need not be cited because in every case the paper that favours protection is recommended as the medium through which to advertise.
No less interesting than the Analysis and the Key, and even more informative, are the reports issued confidentially to the subscribers to Mr. Murray's service. In a sheet called Editor and Publisher, dated August 28, 1920, appears one of these reports :
Toronto-G. M. Murray, whose plan for putting control of the editorial opinion of Canadian newspapers into the hands of the purchasers of advertising was reported last spring in Editor and Publisher and given liberal space in the Canadian press, is "in again." He attributes his previous lack of success to the fact that newspapers did not then need the money so badly as they do now, in the face of rapidly rising costs. Under date of August 16, in his latest "confidential" communication to the manufacturers he is trying to organize, he says: "What with one thing and another, the newspapers were simply reaping a harvest and if an advertiser tried to talk editorial policy to them, they simply wouldn't listen."
"Just when they are beginning to figure how much higher they can jack up their advertising rates to meet their increased cost of production and to calculate how much more space they oan sell at the higher rates, along comes a business depression that leads to the wholesale slashing of advertising appropriations. To the manufacturer in a similar position, the sympathetic editor would no douibt say, 'Draw on your reserve.' But it makes a wonderful difference whose ox is being gored.

"Advertisers can talk policy to that editor today and they will he attentively listened to. The editor knows that advertisers form the one class who can save his enterprise from financial disaster and anything those advertisers ask in reason they are going to get.
"The fact that already there have disappeared from the field such papers as the Toronto News, Peterborough Review, Saskatoon Phoenix and Regina Post is warning to all and sundry that in the midst of journalistic life we are in death and that he who would survive must henceforth pay less attention to the editorial sanctum and more to the office of the business manager."
Having thus pointed out to the manufacturers how they could bring the newspapers to time Mr. Murray proceeded to goad them to action and on December 29, 1920, he sent out a report in which the following paragraph occurred:
To-day the free trade storm signals are set as a warning to navigators upon the sea of business. Make no mistake about it. They are there to be seen, clear as the sun in the sky, by all except those who keep their heads in the sand. The organized farmers, under the leadership of fanatical theorists, have been worked up into a veritable frenzy of resentment against a fiscal policy that they have come to look upon as special privilege. They are out to effect changes by a process of destruction-a process that once initiated may go to untold lengths before it can be checked. If those who would thus be destroyed don't speedily organize for their own defence, and marshall all their resources in money and brains to meet the attack, they will almost certainly find themselves powerless to ward off a blow for which the Grain Grower arm is already bared, nerved with the last ounce of strength and determination.
In another - communication to the subscribers on the subject of how they should spend their advertising appropriation in 1921 Mr. Murray said:
"The average agent, of course, pays little or no attention to editorial policy; with him all that counts is rates and circulation. If he had his way, many a publication that is doing its best to ruin Canadian industry, would be rewarded by the prospective victims to its folly with huge chunks of profitable business, tendered on a silver piatter. I try to persuade my subscribers to let me look over the schedules their agents are asking them to adopt. When they comply, I give them a brief report upon every publication in the list. Those that are O.K. are marked accordingly. In the case of those that are objectionable, I explain what it is that makes them objectionable. Some are worse than others. Some I recommend be retained, but with a reduction from full to part schedule. Some I recommend dropping altogether, and to replace them I submit where possible the names of meritorious publications of a similar class circulating in the same territory."
''The far-reaching possibilities of this work are nicely illustrated in an unsolicited letter just received from an old friend connected with a paper that has been giving us splendid support. Speaking of one contemporary (a low tariff advocate) he says it has noticeably moderated In tone, in an effort to hold all the advertising
231J
it can. Speaking of another (a free-trade organ) he says that despite many manifestations of wrath, as it lost schedule after schedule, it now appears to be tactfully backing away from free trade. 'If your work', he continues, 'has had one-half the effect in other parts of Canada that it has had here, then your subscribers should be able to See it as I do. Moreover, an opportunity for increasing its effectiveness will come with the new year, when newsprint costs will take a further jump, and the difficulties of the publishing business will grow more acute. Many papers will watch their step, more particularly so because they know through past publicity that you exist and are watching things'."
"This frank statement of the case should sure-* ly suggest to all subscribers the desirability of refraining from entering into any new advertising contracts until they have first submitted their schedules to me for a report."
Now, Sir, as a final link in the chain I will summarize the details of a few incidents that establish the connection between Mr. Murray's operations and the Canadian Manufacturers' Association.
At a meeting held in Toronto last year it was represented by the executive of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association that a fund of $3,000,000 would have to be available in the event of a Dominion election. Of this sum it was stated that $1,000,000 should be immediately available. A difficulty arose on the score that companies or corporations were debarred from making political subscriptions; but this was overcome by the explanation that the money would be used chiefly for newspaper propaganda.
Mr. Murray was present at this meeting, and after explaining his plans for securing protectionist publicity, he obtained the approval of the meeting for his method of distributing among the newspapers "ready prints" or "patent insides". Mr. Murray was placed in charge of this work, and it was decided to supply all the funds that were necessary to make it a success. So that the Canadian Manufacturers' Association might not be officially connected with the scheme, a special committee was appointed to deal with it, and an amount, said to have been in the neighbourhood of $40,000, was placed at the disposal of this special committee. It was emphasized that the association would look to Mr. Murray to protect its interests, and that the greatest possible care should be taken to prevent the attitude of the manufacurers towards the newspapers from being made public.
For the present, Mr. Speaker, I do not consider it necessary to enter into any further details of the operations of Mr. Murray and his protectionist patrons. In all probability I have gone far enough to make it unlikely that any supporter of the

Government will rise in his place to defend the methods that I have just exposed; and yet, Sir, it must be borne in mind that these methods are being resorted to for the political benefit of the party now in office, and that that party must share responsibility for these methods with those who originate them, must share responsibility with those who finance them, and must share responsibility with those who carry them into execution to the detriment of the national welfare.
Mr. Speaker, it is because I hold these and the other opinions that I have expressed in the course of my address that I shall vote for the amendment that has been placed in your hands after being moved by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's.
Sir, in the next general election the whole record of the present Government will be the issue before the public. The Government's tariff policy will form an important part of that record. Hence, Sir, it is the duty of all who desire to see peace, prosperity and goodwill restored in this country to acquaint the electors at every possible opportunity with the true inwardness of the Government's tariff policy and with the aims and methods of those who support it. East Elgin and West Peterborough have demonstrated, and I venture to prophesy, without fear of successful contradiction, that York-Sunbury, Yamaska and Medicine Hat will further demonstrate, that protection will not protect this Government from the fate that awaits it when the verdict of the whole Canadian people is registered at the polls.

speakeroldname: Hon. S. F. TOLMIE (Minister of Agriculture) :
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to take part in this debate but for the fact that the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) in the course of his speech made certain statements with reference to the building of a dry dock at Esquimalt, B.C. He implied that the construction of this drydock was entered upon for the purpose of assisting my re-election after my appointment as Minister of Agriculture. I want to state here, Sir, that if I had felt it was necessary to have a dry dock or any other public work constructed to elect me as a member of this House, I would still be in the live stock business out on the Pacific slope. I am quite sure that the hon. gentleman did not possess full information on the subject or he would not have made the statement which he placed before this House, and on that account I think it would be well for me to give the
[Mr. Murphy.J
history of the construction of the dry dock from its inception up to the present time.
Esquimalt is located about four miles from Victoria at the southern extremity of Vancouver Island. It is in the constituency of the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. McIntosh). I represent the city of Victoria alone. A small dock, about 430 feet in length, was constructed at Esquimalt about forty years ago, for the purpose of accommodating naval vessels, Esquimalt having been the station of the British Navy on the Pacific coast for a number of years until it was handed over by the Imperial authorities to the Canadian Government. The dock was found of excellent service, and was the means of establishing at that particular point a very important ship repairing and shipbuilding business. For a long time, however, it had been felt that owing to the increasing size of vessels it was necessary to have a larger dry dock, for in many instances the Esquimalt dock being unable to accommodate ships wishing to dock for repairs, those ships went over to United States dry docks, and the work was lost to our contractors and also to our workingmen.
About the year 1912 the question of a drydock became a live issue. The matter was discussed very freely and active measures were taken to induce the Government to take some action with a view to providing larger accommodation in the dry-dock line. Til fact that same year a dry-dock site was purchased at Lang's Cove in Esquimalt Harbour. About that time a big shipbuilding firm, Yarrows, Limited, with headquarters at Glasgow, Scotland, was searching about the Pacific coast for a suitable site for a drydock, having in view the establishment of a branch of their business on this continent. They examined sites on the American as well as on the Canadian side and after a thorough investigation they decided that Esquimalt was the most suitable place for their dry-dock. It may be of interest to hon. members to know that that was just five years before I had contemplated going into politics at all. The dock site, as I say, was selected, but owing to the fact that the war broke out shortly afterwards the work was not proceeded with and no further active steps were taken until 1919, the construction of the dock being agreed to in the month of June of that year. It was not until August 2 that I was asked to accept the portfolio of agriculture in the present government when the construction of the dock was ' agreed to in June.

I had no more idea of occupying my present position than I had of leaving for some other country; nor was the matter brought to my attention in any way by any member of the Government. It was 1920 that the contract was let for the construction of this dock. I cannot see, therefore, how under these circumstances my election either in 1919 or in 1917 can be connected with the construction of this dry-dock at Esquimalt.
Another dock is to be built at Vancouver under the Drydock Subsidies Act. There is also a floating dock at Prince Rupert, owned by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, but as that point is over 500 miles north of Victoria ships will not go from the south end of Vancouver island or down in the neighbourhood of the Straits of Juan de Fuca up as far as Prince Rupert if they can secure satisfactory accommodation nearer at hand.
There are a number of reasons why" Esquimalt has been selected as the site for this drydock. A glance at the map will show that the Straits of Juan de Fuca pass in from the Pacific eastward and branch off to the south, terminating in Puget Sound on the American side, and also pass up to the .north and into the Gulf of Georgia, thence up to Vancouver and further north. Esquimalt is situated about fifty miles from the Pacific ocean, and all traffic, whether destined for Southern Columbia ports or for American ports, passes practically within view of Esquimalt harbour, so that we have the benefit not only of Canadian-bound but also of American-bound traffic. The port is practically free from fog the year round. The waters of Esquimalt harbour have a considerable advantage over those of eastern points where drydocks are located in that they are liquid during the whole year, making them always navigable. We have there a very light rainfall, from 27 to 32 inches in the average year. Last year there was an average of sunshine or bright weather from five and a half to six hours a day during the whole year. There is winter temperature of about 42 degrees and a summer temperature of 60 degrees enabling men to work on the ships the year round; no fires are necessary to keep the men warm during the winter season. The work can be carried on under the cheapest possible conditions. The port is situated advantageously in that help can be secured from nearby centres, where it is always available, in the event of any big rush of ship repairing work coming on at any particular time.
About the time that the dry dock site was purchased Yarrows Limited was given to understand that this dock was to be constructed at Esquimalt, and this big firm immediately decided that they would, locate there. They have since been carrying on to great advantage the business of a ship repair plant, employing a large number of men. The Government have thus not only kept faith with the people of Victoria, to whom this dock had been promised but have also kept faith with this big British firm which had come to this country to invest its money. If we hope to get British capital in this country one of the first things we must do is to carry out our undertakings in respect to that capital on every possible occasion. About seven or eight weeks ago I made a hurried trip to Victoria and Esquimalt, and at that time they had four deep sea-going vessels under repair. They had recently turned down another vessel because they could not accommodate it, and a Japanese vessel, the Manila Maru, had to go to Seattle for dockage accommodation because that available at Esquimalt was to small. This firm have plenty of capital. They do not ask for bonuses; if they lose money on a contract nobody knows anything about it but themselves; they do not come to the Government for assistance. They are rapidly building up a very valuable business at that point and employing a' large number of Canadian workmen.
The trade of the Pacific Coast is increasing at a very rapid rate. There is at present about $2,000,000,000 worth of trade carried on yearly between America and Canadian Pacific ports and the Orient and countries to the south, and with the many millions of people over on the Asiatic side it is only reasonable to expect that this trans-Pacific business will increase by leaps and bounds, If we are to meet the situation we must have proper facilities on the Canadian side to accommodate shipping, to repair ships, and so on. As an indication of how keenly alive the Americans are to the situation, let me say that they have no less than sixteen floating and graving docks situated at San Francisco, Seattle, Portland, Oregon, and Bremerton, Washington, as compared with our one small dock at Esquimalt, which accommodates only one small ship, one floating dock at Prince Rupert and two other docks under construction. In the East, too, there are a larger number of docks than there are on the Pacific Coast. From the figures I will give you in a moment you will see that the number of docks on the Pacific is very

small compared with that in the East, having regard to the amount of tonnage involved. With the present dock at Esqui-malt and one under construction we will be able to accommodate any ship afloat. The dock has a division in the centre so that two small ships can be put in at the same time giving us dock accommodations for three vessels at once. Through the operations of this firm of Yarrows Limited, which is known from one end of the world
to the other where shipping is done, I am sure that a great deal of business will be brought to that point once it is known that we can accommodate anything that may offer.

I do not believe that the country is going to gain very much by our continually voicing our pessimism, or talking about hard times. By intelligent expansion, the country can accomplish a great deal of good. Having been brought up in the West and having experienced one or two western real estate booms, I ido not feel at all down-hearted about our present condition. By careful economy, by the investment of money along such lines as give promise of safe development, this country is absolutely Sure in its future progress. In addition to that, I feel that after what we have accomplished in the war, we have the proper Canadian spirit to develop and build up a country which must occupy a position of prominence amongst the great nations. This is one of the finest countries in the world, and our present conditions will compare very favourably with those existing in any other country that has taken part in the war.
Mr. FERNAND RINFRET (St. James:) Mr. Speaker, after the contribution made to this debate to-day by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy), I feel there is very little to say on this side of the House, and I rise only to put myself on record as briefly as possible regarding this Budget which is of such interest to the people of the riding that I represent. The Prime Minister the other day in the' course of this debate made the statement that he did not think in the whole of his parliamentary career he had witnessed a budget statement received with such general approval as that of this year. I humbly submit that this is another case which should come under the ruling of the Chair against imaginary statements'being recorded in Hansard. I consider, on the contrary, that never in the history of this country has there been presented to the House a budget so appalling in figures, so disastrous in all that it has to admit and certainly none so burdensome upon the Canadian taxpayer. The Minister of Finance has	to admit	that

although he has exerted his power of taxation with a view to securing from the public $100,000,000 more than is needed for the current expenditure of the country nevertheless on the whole operations of the year the deficit is twice that amount. The Minister of Finance, however, has great confidence in the future. With this distressing statement, he has given the House the valuable information that the sun still shines, our rivers still sparkle, our lands are as great and as fertile as ever, and our resources just as vast. Alas, Mr. Speaker, he has forgotten to add that our Federal expenditures are as great as ever, our deficits are running up all the time and the Government of the country is as incompetent and as unrepresentative as ever. Not that I wish to lay the whole blame on the. Minister of Finance. We all know that he has only joined the Government of late, and that he is not responsible for most of the trouble. When he joined the Government party boat, to borrow a familiar metaphor of the Prime Minister, the ship of State was in a very unseaworthy condition, with the sails all torn out, the bottom leaking lamentably, the oars half disabled, and the planks in such a state of rottenness that no one short of a magician could have restored it and put it back into sailing condition. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance, though a sinner, is only a sinner of the eleventh hour, and I do hope that for him the text of scripture does not apply in the reverse form. He has done his best under the circumstances. He labours under the burden of an intolerable legacy, and is hampered by a policy which has proven disastrous. What could he do in view of the railway policy of the Government, and the merchant marine, the Militia Estimates, and all the extravagances of the Government? It is only natural to find that his financial powers have been superseded, and it is only logical that he should find himself confronted today with a shortage of food and an excess of appetite.
While the Minister of Finance undertook the duty of telling the people by what amount the country has been impoverished during the past year, the Prime Minister took upon himself to enter upon what he called a discussion of the tariff. May I here interject with all due courtesy that while we paid the greatest attention to the speech of the right hon. the Prime Min-* ister, even to the point of putting questions to him occasionally, I was surprised to find that when the leader of the OppositMi\ Kinfret.]

I think it is very seldom that a speech has been delivered by the leader of either party in a Budget debate wihch the other leader has not followed with due attention.

In the meantime, the Prime Minister is leaving for England and, as I understand, he will deliver a few speeches there. I have no doubt that he will make the best use of his knowledge and talent when he addresses the British public. Now, he alluded the other day to the speech he delivered on the Budget last year. That speech contained a description of the way in which the fiscal policy of England has operated in the Mother Country, and I would advise my right hon. friend to take that speech with him when he goes there and quote it. I can picture the scene at the great banquet where all the economists of the country would be gathered and when the traditional usher would call in his rich melodious voice "silence, pray, for the Prime Minister of Canada." My right hon. friend would get up and say:
3Vty Lords and Gentlemen, you are all wrong and your fiscal policy is all wrong. Free trade has depopuated rural England; it has filled the emigrant ships with fugitives from her shores: it has scattered the manhood of Great Britain through the fields and workshops of the United States it has starved and repressed and dwarfed the nascent industries of Ireland ; it has reversed the supremacy that Britain held through centuries In the industrial life of the world, and caused her to concede the place to other great competing nations who adopted a different policy. Such is the history of free trade.
Now, I will not play the childish trick of waiting for the question to be asked, "Who said or wrote this?" This is a speech that was delivered by the Prime Minister. It was not written by Norman Lambert; it is a speech to which the Prime Minister gave utterance.

I know that. That
speech last year evoked a great deal of applause from the other side-in fact everything my right hon. friend says evokes a great deal of applause and desk-thumping on that side. Unfortunately that deskthumping has no echo in the country; its only effect is to injure the furniture in the chamber and further add *to the prevailing waste and extravagance. But I do not think there will be any desk-thumping in England if the Prime Minister repeats those sentiments there. If I have quoted his speech it is not for the mere pleasure of including it in the debate. It is because we find there in that single paragraph that blind, partisan, prejudiced attachment to a fiscal policy that we precisely condemn in the amendment that is before the House. I would go further than that. As far as I

am concerned I will say that I not only approve of the amendment as it stands, but I would make it read: that the tariff should not be based on the principle of protection, or on the principle of free trade, or on any stringent fixed doctrine. Because I contend, Mr. Speaker, that in this country-young and rising as it is-we cannot fix the tariff on any stringent doctrine: It must be flexible, it must be dealt with item by item, and it must adapt itself to the needs of the country.

At this late hour I do n6t propose to detain the House very much longer. Some of the details of the Budget are very interesting. For example there has been quite a change in connection with the Customs Department, and I wish to congratulate the Minister of Customs upon having given up the writing of private letters and busying himself with public affairs. We are promised a chance in the Customs Department that we on this side have been asking for a long time in order to put that department on a business basis.' Last year we inquired whether the Government intended to estimate customs duties according to the current rate of exchange and the reply was made by the then Minister of Customs that they did not. But good ideas make their way. On July 22, the former system was altered and a regulation passed by Order in Council-the usual method of the Government in dealing with these matters, only it was too long delayed-changing the regulations of the department in that respect. This session the Minister of Customs was asked whether further changes were intended as regards, for instance, goods coming from the United States, and again the reply was in the negative. However, good ideas once more made their way. We are now told that this regulation will also apply to imports of goods from the United States. Unfortunately the Government has seen fit to put an arbitrary value on all European moneys in this sense-that it will not, in any case, allow the depreciation to be any lower than 50 per cent. Now it is a well-known fact, Mr. Speaker, that European merchants who are quite conversant with the depreciation of their money usually make an overcharge on their goods before they export them to this country. However, this is a matter which can be taken up more in detail when we reach the committee stage. The same applies to the sales taxes and other provisions of the Budget.
Before I take my seat I wish to say a word or two about what is embodied in the last

clause of the amendment concerning the general expenditure of the country. I think we should divide that expenditure into two groups. The first group would include expenditure, which we must acknowledge because it forms obligations which the country has taken upon itself. In this group would be the war debt, and I fully share what was so eloquently stated by the hon. member for Megantic (Mr. Pacaud) that as regards war expenditure we must pay up without the least discussion. But, Mr. Speaker, I think we should not altogether allow ourselves to be too much moved by the mere fact that it is war expenditure, because it is well known that under that head are included not only the amounts that were strictly necessary for the conduct of the war, but also considerable amounts which represent the scandalous and extravagant waste which was indulged in during that time. I am not going over all that again. It was proven in this House and before the Public Accounts Committee that millions of dollars were squandered in payments to profiteers-friends of the Government, colonels and others. Therefore although we must pay that debt, we should be allowed to hold the Government responsible for the fact that we are not only paying interest on strictly war expenditure, but we are also paying interest on all those millions which were squandered. We should also hold the Government responsible, although I am afraid we cannot remedy the evil, for the fact that $1,300,000,000 were invested in loans which are exempt from income tax. I need not say that profiteers who had made enormous profits during the war and did not know where to invest their money were the first to take advantage of these war loans. I remember an article which I once read in an American paper to the effect that you ought always to keep a very close watch on profiteers because of their alertness. The writer went on to say that in a certain country it had been decided to hang profiteers, and those profiteers at once formed a trust to hoard coffins! That is what the people can expect from profiteers. But there is another group of expenditures, and they have been mentioned often during the course of this debate. There is, for instance, the railway deficit. I see my good friend-if I dare use that expression-the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) before me, and I recall when I was a member of the press gallery in the old House how he used to get up with feigned indignation when the Intercolonial railway was showing i'AIi. a deficit of a few million dollars. Mr. Speaker, we have read in that great poem, Dante's "Inferno", that the sinners were punished according to the character of their sins; the gluttons were famished, the proud were humiliated, and carnal sinners were tortured in their very flesh. I think, Sir, that my good friend has reached a circle where, after feeling so indignant over a deficit of a few million dollars, he has now to swallow a deficit of $75,000,000 or $100,000,000 as the result of his Government's policy.
