But I do recall that
recently when the genial Minister of Marine was showing us over a dry dock-not the Victoria dry dock, but a dry dock in Maisonneuve-he took great pride in the fact that they were launching a boat which was being sold to Norway for $170 a ton. When the minister made that remark a member said-I do not know if it reached the ear of the minister-"If that is so, by all means let him sell the merchant ships of the Government and get rid of them as soon as he can at that price." As for the Militia Estimates, it is no argument to declare that we are not spending more for the militia than we did before the war. As a matter of fact we are spending more. But the argument of the Minister of Militia and Defence (Mr. Guthrie) was that as the militia was more costly now than before the war we had to spend more on it for the same number of men. I have figures here-but I will not go over them now which show that we have more employees now in the Militia Department and about one thousand more men in the force than we had before the war. We should do away with this militia expenditure because it is less needed at the present time, because it is more costly, and because we have no money to waste on it.
I have tried, Mr. Speaker, to go over the different clauses of the amendment, but there is one reason more than any other which will lead me to vote for that amendment, and that is that it contains a general denunciation of the policy of the Government, and if perchance it were carried it would force the Government to go to the country, and would restore to the hands of the people their supreme and paramount right to elect their own representatives.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to detain the

House very long, but some statements have been made that I think I should answer. Before doing so I want to compliment the Minister of Finance on his splendid Budi get report. I think never in the history of this House has there been presented a Budget so acceptable to the people or so eulogized even by members opposite. I also feel glad that in our Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) Canada has such an able leader, . and when I read some of the eulogistic statements made by hon. gentlemen opposite regarding the Prime Minister, I feel" that we on this side of the House have reason to be very proud of him indeed.
There has been a great change in my time in the official Opposition. I have been a member since 1904, and at that time there was a solid Liberal delegation from British Columbia supporting Sir Wilfrid Laurier-that great and respected statesman whom I think every one remembers to with pride. Where is that representation to-day? Not one is left. Hon. gentlemen opposite have lost the support of that solid delegation. In Alberta the same condition exists-only one or two supporters of the Liberal party have been returned by that province; in Saskatchewan you find the same condition; and in the province of Manitoba their support . has all gone to pieces. So we can say without possibility of contradiction that the great western provinces which supported the policy of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier and of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) have deserted the present official leader of the party. Indeed, I think I am right in saying that outside of the province of Quebec he and his party have from the other provinces only twenty or twenty-one supporters in this House. As against that, on this side of the House supporting the Government we have about thirty of the stalwart old Liberals whose names are well known throughout all Canada as the very foundation and pillars of Liberalism in the past.
They will never come back.

Well, my hon. friend may not be as good a prophet as he thinks he is, I could recall the names of some of these men. Take men like William Charlton, from a neighbouring county of mine, one of the stalwart Liberals in Ontario during the last fifty years and a strong supporter of the present Government. We have the Mowats the descendants of Blake-we
have all the great Liberals of the province standing by and supporting this Government. We on this side are a united, enthusiastic and loyal party, and we are loyal and enthusiastic in the support of our present Prime Minister, whom we are proud to follow.
I want to refer just for a moment to the Agrarian group. I do not want to say anything unkind of them. I have respect for them; I have respect for the farmers of this country. No man in this House sympathizes more with the farmers than I do. I know how hard they work for their money; I know what long hours they devote to their work on the farm; I know the conditions under which they live. But I submit that hon. gentlemen on this side are all anxious and willing to do what they can for the farming interests of Caada. So far as I am concerned, if the Farmers' party on any other party in this House will move a resolution which in my judgment is in the interests of the farming people of this country I will support it. But we do not get many of those resolutions. We hear many statements and a lot of talk, but we do not get very many resolutions from hon. gentlemen oposite.
One of the great questions in this country, a few years ago, as you know, Mr. Speaker, was conscription. I do not want to refer at any length to that subject, but I am sorry that the Government of Canada had to enforce conscription. The conditions were such, as hon. gentlemen of the Agrarian Party know, that the decision to enforce conscription had to be supported, and who helped to support it? The leader of the Agrarian Party and the men sitting behind him crossed the floor of the House, supported conscription and voted in support of this Government for at least two years. They did that, I say in the interests of enforcing conscription in this country, and I want that put on record in order that the farmers of my county, anyway, may know that we were not alone on this side of the House with regard to that question.
We have heard a good deal in this House about free trade. As the' Prime Minister has said, I think that free trade was born in the West. In that part of the country some of the people are pretty sincere, perhaps, in the views which they hold on free trade. But I have sat in this House with a good many of those who now make up the Agrarian party. Where were they in the years when the tariff of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding)

was carried out in this country? Where were they during those sixteen years? That tariff was higher than the tariff at present in force, because reductions have since been made by this Government on many of the necessities of life, upon agricultural implements especially. But even when the tariff was higher, every one of the representatives of the farmers in this House supported that policy and helped to carry it out-the high tariff policy of the member for Shelburne and Queen's. None of them went back on it at that time; they seemed to think it was all right. The reason is that they were supporting a low tariff policy then; they were supporting a high tariff policy. And my friends directly opposite are in precisely the same position. They talk now about free trade and the tariff, but between 1896 and 1911 they supported the policy of the member for Shelburne and Queen's and stood by it by their votes and their speeches in this House. I want to congratulate the member for Shelburne and Queen's upon the fiscal policy which he maintained during thdse years; I wish that the Liberal party sitting behind the present leader of the Opposition would stand by the principles that Sir Wilfrid Laurier and the member for Shelburne and Queen's upheld during all those years. We who are interested in manufacturing and in supporting the manufacturing industries would be proud indeed if we could look forward to the continuance of such a policy as the Liberal party had at that time. But I doubt very much whether on the Liberal side of the House we have a great many men, especially among those from the province of Quebec, who would be glad to suport that policy or who if they were returned to power-even with the Agrarian's, the annex supporting them- would see that ,the principle was carried out. They talk of free trade, but I do not believe they are free traders at all, the great bulk of them. I do not believe they have an idea in their mind of lowering the tariff. A great many of the members from Quebec, especially those from Montreal, including the member for St. James Division (Mr. Rinfret) who has just spoken, would not support any policy which had in view the lowering of the tariff. The same applies to many other memb'ers who have spoken on this question. The member for West Peterborough (Mr. Gordon)-does any one think that he is a low tariff man or a free trader? Not by any means; he is a supporter of high tariff, or

would be if he thought that any proposed tariff for Canada would have the effect of intefering with the progress and development of the manufacturing industries of this country.
I do not think any class of the people would be in a worse position with a low tariff than the farmers would be. The protection of the farming interests is necessary especially in Ontario. I do not believe there is any sympathy so far as the tariff is concerned between the farmers of Western Canada and the farmers of Ontario and Quebec; their ideas are entirely different. The farmers of the West depend upon wheat and grains almost entirely; the farmers of Ontario depend upon general farming and as general farmers they never could stand for free trade or a low tariff duties on farm products. Take the question of butter and eggs. The amount of butter imported from the United States last year was very large. We imported 7,000,000 dozen of eggs from the United States, and $10,000,000 worth of meats last year; do hon. gentlemen say that the tariff should be lowered and more of these goods imported? A large number of the farmers of my county were at one time in favour of reciprocity, but when they heard the arguments presented to them, when they realized the condition in which they would be placed under a low tariff or under reciprocity with the United States, they voted very strongly against it. And what did reciprocity do for them in respect of the articles on which it was applied? It did not help them any in the manufactdr-ing line, as we all know, because the duties to-day upon agricultural implements necessary for use on the farm are lower than as provided for under the reciprocity agreement. So that reciprocity, I say, would not be any advantage to them. I say without fear of contradiction that a protective tariff-that is, a fairly reasonable protective tariff-is in the interests of the farmers of Quebec. We have heard many misrepresentations in connection with the -manufacturing industries. I say that the manufacturing industries of this country are misrepresented by statements made by the Agrarian group as well as by the official Opposition. So far as hon. gentlemen opposite are concerned I do not believe they are sincere in the statements which they make; they surely must be in favour of reasonable protection to the manufacturing industries of Canada. Quebec is a great manufacturing province, one of the greatest in Canada, and I am sure that

Quebec will grow in importance and in wealth under a fair and reasonable protective tariff. What would a low tariff do as regards people who work in factories? It would, as we all know, throw them out of employment, and I am sure men working in factories need protection now if they ever needed it in their history, when men are out of employment and looking for work. I regret exceedingly that there is unemployment in Canada to-day. But what would be the result if you took down the tariff wall between the United States and Canada, and with a low tariff or free trade allowed goods to come into this country? Hon. members from Quebec and the other provinces know as well as I do what would happen. I know that in my town in which I have lived all my life, if it were not for the manufacturers and industries in that town, grass would almost grow upon its streets. It is a town that has grown in a few years from a population of about 1,500 to something like 4,000, as the result of reasonable protection to its manufacturing industries.
Hon. gentlemen opposite say that manufacturers increase the price, I say that such is not the case. If you want to lower the price to the consumers of Canada, manufacture the goods in your own country, and competition between manufacturers in Canada will reduce the price to the level of the price of the imported article. Every dollar's worth of goods made in the United States or Great Britain and imported into Canada displaces just so much goods made in Canada and throws Canadians out of employment to that extent. My hon. friend shakes his head, but that is certainly the case. Men cannot be upheld in manufacturing industries; families cannot be kept and encouraged, unless manufacturers have a reasonable profit to encourage their industries. Manufacturers, we are told, take advantage of the duty and add it to the price. As a manufacturer, I say that that statement is not founded on fact; manufacturers do not take into consideration the duty upon an article when they set the price. What regulates the price is competition amongst manufacturers themselves, and perhaps the hon. member for Waterloo North (Mr. Euler) will bear me out in that. As I said, competition amongst manufacturers is sufficient to make the price just as low as it possibly can be made, and the price is very low and close. On many articles in Canada we manufacture and sell just as cheaply as American manufacturers do. I
believe that in this country, boots and shoes-and they can go into the United States free of duty-can be bought just as cheaply as in the United States, and surely it is better to employ our people making shoes rather than to employ Americans to make them. I do not think members from Quebec, with the great shoe industries of that province, would ever endorse or support a policy that would admit boots and shoes into this country under a low tariff or free trade.
The same thing applies to the textile industry. Hon. gentlemen opposite tell us that we should appoint trade commissioners to develop trade in the United States. How can you develop trade in the United States for our manufactured goods when they put up a tariff wall that shuts us out of their market. A duty of 30 to 40 per cent is imposed on textiles going into the United .States. How can you get over that wall of protection, and what would trade commissioners do in that country to develop and increase the exports of Canada? The people of the United States do not want our goods; their whole policy is to keep them out, not only by tariff, but by regulation, and any man who has attempted to export goods to the United States knows that the regulations there impose such restrictions upon him that it is almost impossible to get his goods in. I know, from experience, that textiles are sold as cheaply in Canada as in the United States. I am interested in a large factory in Buffalo in the United States; our scale of wages in Canada is practically the same as that in our American factory, and the goods we manufacture in our different factories in Canada are just about as cheap in price as those manufactured in our factory, and the goods we manufacture in factory in the United States. We do not sell our goods in the United States any cheaper than we do in Canada, so that the people of Canada are not robbed to the extent of one cent as against American prices. But we employ about 1,000 people in this country with their families to manufactories, and we must remember that those goods are made in 'Canada. Surely, that is better than manufacturing them in the United States and bringing them into Canada. If you import goods from the United States or from England, the people pay the price and the duty also. The development of industry in Canada will make our price lower than the American price and will encourage the employment of our own people.

What do the people of the United States contribute to our country and its development? They do not contribute towards our churches, charities, taxes, or anything else; but they manufacture goods and ship them in here, employing their people while, when goods are manufactured in Canada, that means that Canadians are employing their own people and contributing money towards Canadian necessities.
I was much amused the other day at the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) saying that taxes should be imposed upon vacant lots. I do not think the hon. gentleman is sincere in that. In my town and in every other town and city in Canada artisans working in factories and men employed in other walks of life have bought lots; they are trying to save up enough money to pay for those lots and eventually to build a home on them, and the hon. member for Marquette says that those lots should be taxed in the interest of the Federal Government. I do not think the working people of Canada would appreciate very much a statement of that kind.
We want the Canadian market for the Canadian people, whether it is the manufacturer, artisan, man or woman working in those factories. We have about 8,000,000 people in this country. Do our own friends opposite say that we should open up that market of 8,000,000 people to the 105,000,000 people in the United States? As a manufacturer I say-and I think the manufacturers of Canada would endorse what I say,-that if we could get into that market free of duty, we would hold up both our hands for that; but they will not let us in; they shut us out, by their tariff and regulations. Yet our hon. friends says: "Let them into our market and ruin our market and industries for the Canadian people." That is not a loyal or patriotic policy for Canada. Every town, I think, wants manufacturing industries, and we want to encourage the establishment and development of such industries; but the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) says: "If you know of any individual or institution who wants to come to Canada and start a manufacturing industry, tell him not to come."

tariff.

He says: " They will not get any protection in this country if they come. If you know of anybody in Canada who contemplates starting an enterprise, tell him not to start one because he will not

get reasonable protection." I say that all Canadian towns and even our cities want protection and to encourage and induce manufacturing industries to locate in them. In my town, the board of trade and Municipal council are putting forth efforts every day in an endeavour to ge manufacturers to locate there. Under the policy of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), they are told to keep away and not to start their manufacturing industries in Canada.

I think so, that if the
manufacturer depended upon protection he had better keep away. I say that we want to depend on protection. We want industries started in this country. We want men in Canada who have enterprise enough to start new industries, and there are a good many men in Canada who are abused by hon. gentlemen opposite who have enterprise enough to invest their money in Cana' dian industries. There are many men in this country who started with a very small capital, and who by their enterprise have built up manufacturing industries that are a credit to Canada. One of the great industries that I am interested in is the knitting business. We have a large institution which grew up under the Liberal policy in this country which gave us ample protection. All that we asked was that they would announce their intention of continuing that policy. Unfortunately, however, the Liberal party have now reached this position: They are afraid of the Agrarian group, who are free traders, and in order to satisfy them if they possibly can, they take the position in their speeches, at all events, in favour of low tariff or free trade. Whether they are sincere in that, I cannot say, but I doubt

very much if they are. I believe, however, that many people in Canada believe that they are insincere. They know what the Liberal' party professed in this country previous to 1896, when they were preaching this kind of thing, but did not carry it out after they had got into power. They put on a tariff very much higher than the tariff of this Government. The tariff of this Government is at least 3 per cent lower than the tariff of the Liberal party. I ask hon. gentlemen opposite, if they are restored to power, would they restore the tariff. That shows how sincere they were, in power, and would our Agrarian friends support it? Our Agrarian friends who had loyally supported this Government left this side of the House when we lowered the tariff. That shows how insincere they were. I believe that the friends of the official Opposition throughout the country think that if they are returned to power they will not lower the tariff. I do not know what would happen between the two groups opposite. I do not know who would be leader, the hon. member for Prince (Mr. King), or the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar). There may be some trouble over that, but at present both parties are trying to stand upon the resolution and the policy that has been introduced by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's. His resolution does not mean anything. Members from Ontario and Quebec, free traders and protectionists can all stand on that resolution.
Since I have been in this House I have never heard any one in the Farmers group move a resolution in favour of their policy of low tariff and free trade. I have never heard a resolution moved by the official'Opposition in this House advocating low tariff or free trade. They have not the courage to move such a resolution. The Prime Minister has dared them time and again to do it, but they have not done so. They have simply indulged in vague statements, instead of bringing in a resolution upon which one could stand.
I rose chiefly for the purpose of speaking on a matter in connection with which my name has been mentioned. I refer to the Roumanian and Greek orders. The men who have made that statement have made a statement that is absolutely unfair, and it was made for political purposes. I want to give the Farmers group credit. I do not think they have made that statement; but our friends of the official Opposition have. What are the facts? I speak of the industry I am interested in-the textile business. Samples were submitted by the Canadian manufacturers to Roumania and Greece. They themselves selected from those samples certain goods that they wanted to buy from Canada; they were a pretty low-priced goods. They sent their men over here, and they met manufacturers from every province. I say without hesitation and without fear of contradiction that no pressure or influence was brought to bear by any manufacturer to secure orders under the Roumanian or Greek loans. The manufacturers were given orders just as large as they could handle, and in some eases more. At the meeting of the manufacturers each one had the privilege of taking all the orders he could supply, and as I said before, manufacturers were there from Quebec, Montreal and every province and every place where they manufacture textile goods. Our manufacturers were busy at the time manufacturing goods for thp home market, and many took orders beyond their capacity. Other firms had to take over these contracts later. We manufactured what we had contracted for, and we helped out a good many other manufacturers, but there was no pressure or influence whatever brought to bear. It was a Clean, fair arrangement to everybody who wanted to take an order, regardless of what province he came from or where he made the goods. I say that it is absolutely unfair for men, solely for political purposes, to drag my name and the names of others before this House and claim that we got these orders as a favour from the Government. It was not any favour at all. The manufacturers took these orders largely from patriotic motives/ Notwithstanding that we were pretty busy and could not very well take these orders, the manufacturers felt that it was their duty to take all they could because Roumania and Greece were needing these goods. It was a clean, open business affair, and no one had any favours granted him.
In concluding, I believe that protection is the proper policy for Canada. I am not an extreme protectionist, but I believe that a fair and reasonable protection is in the interests of Canada, in the interests of the farmers, and more particularly in the interests of the working people in the factories of Canada. At the present time industry is in a deplorable condition. I know what I am talking about. Conditions are so bad that some manufacturers have lost more money in the last six months than they made perhaps during the whole of the war. At a time like this, industries need

to be encouraged, and tbe men in those industries should not be held up to ridicule and have unfair statements made about them in this House, because no one deserves such treatment less than those engaged in the manufacturing industries of this country. Our manufacturing industries need help; they need encouragement; they need protection, and I am sorry that all of us, farmers and men in every walk of life, Liberals and Conservatives, cannot all unite upon a policy of support and encouragement to the great manufacturing industries of this country.

GOULD (Assiniboia) : Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland), irf beginning his speech this afternoon, assured the House that he was going tc be exceedingly brief, so that the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) might have the floor immediately. He then proceeded to falsify that prediction, and succeeded admirably in doing so before he took his seat. In contradistinction to the hon. member, when I make the statement now that I shall be brief, I do so with the determination to live up to that assurance, not because there is not enough material to discuss, but because of the very early, or late, hour, as the case may be, and the evident desire of the House to come to a decision upon the question under consideration. That is the principal reason for my intention to be brief in the remarks I am going to make.
Now, the fact has been very patent, not only this session, but last session as well, that there is no single question which has been debated to such an extent from the Government benches as the United Grain Growers' Grain Company. travelled around the country considerably, and I know the sentiment of the people, and I can assure this House that the people, particularly in the western part of Canada, object to these irrational statements on the part of individuals who know little about the operations of that company. I deplore the very low level which was reached by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), in his contribution to the debate. The hon. gentleman's attitude is to be deprecated, and the arguments which he has advanced tonight are not worthy of the smallest man in this House, particularly in so far as his remarks had reference to the United Grain Growers. But there is one matter to which he made reference, and in regard to which I, as an individual, have more information than any other member. I have personal information on the subject in question, and had not been for the fact that the hon. member for Vancouver resuscitated it, I had no! intended to allude to the incident. I know this to be a positive fact, which neither the Prime Minister nor any other gentleman can controvert, for I heard it iterated and reiterated, on the streets of the city of Fredericton, in the committee rooms, and in every other place where men congregate to discuss public matters, that the Government and its party are canvassing absolutely on religious lines. I speak whereof I know, and I would not have referred to this matter had it not been for the efforts of the Government to make it appear that this assertion in the first place had no basis of truth. I repeat that this is the biggest issue discussed
2	a.m. in York-Sunbury, namely the charge that the Government supporters are working on religious grounds.
Now, we have listened to an address on high protection by the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Lalor), and we quite expected the hon. gentleman to make a speech of that nature. I do not think it is necessary for me to enter into any detailed discussion of the merits of the question. The hon. member makes the sweeping assertion that we are free traders. When my hon. friend makes that statement, he thereby gives proof positive that he has not read nor considered the platform on which we stand

Neither he, nor any other hon. gentleman can prove that we have ever stated that we are a free trade party, and yet that assertion is made throughout the country on the hustings, and also in this House, no matter how frequently nor how clearly it is refuted. In a few words, I would say that we demand that those who wish protection shall come before a tribunal of the House and show reasons why they should have it; and that is a most logical position in regard to the tariff. With that sentiment, I will leave any further reply to the statements made by the hon. member for Haldimand.
I rose for the purpose, if possible, at this late hour, of introducing some new material into the debate. Ever since I have come to the House, I have been quite in sympathy with the Minister of Finance in the great task with which he is charged, of raising money wherewith to administer the affairs of the country; but it seems to me that the minister himself is not sympathetic with those who would help him. He apparently has no desire to accept advice from those who tender it from this side of the House, and his cold attitude towards the sincere intentions of hon. members who would lend him some assistance cannot but be regarded as evidence of an improper spirit. Now, I wish to state that I am always proud to say a word for the big organizations of the West, the big agrarian organizations. Some time ago the Saskatchewan Grain Growers' Association asked the Canadian Council of Agriculture to gather first-hand information pending the day when bank legislation would be introduced so that such information could be available for the use of those who might frame that legislation. The idea was borne of a desire to help the Government, but we find that when the Minister of Finance proceeds to get information he does not go to any of these organizations. Now, I am actuated to-night by a desire to suggest to the minister some new avenues whereby money can be raised for the country. My sole desire is to suggest ways and means whereby the Minister of Finance may raise more revenue and tax some sources of wealth so far' untaxed or, if taxed, not taxed to their capacity. I wish to refer, then, to our large banking institutions. Now, the banking institutions of this country, like those of other civilized countries, hold valuable franchises granted by the Government not only for the purpose of handling the moneys of the country, but for extending credits. It is a very valuable thing, a great consideration, to any group of individuals to be granted such a privilege and power. By that power they can extend or curtail expansion, and as a result depress certain industries if they so desire. It seems to me, Sir, that our banking institutions in Canada have not had the right view in respect to commercial and agricultural enterprises. It seems to me that their desire has been to extend credits more quickly to commercial enterprises than they have to agricultural pursuits. I cite the following as an illustration: When we wish to market our wheat in the West, or when, late in the season, it is our desire to prepare the soil for the next season an individual may go to the banks and say "I would like to ask for a loan to permit me to get my land in better shape for my crop of next year. I have so many thousand bushels of wheat threshed and in my bins on the farm and I would like an advance to finance myself until the cold weather comes when I can haul my wheat." Immediately the banking institutions will say "No, we do not extend credit in the case of wheat." But what happens? The moment you take that wheat and put it in the elevators the same banks that in the first instance refused the farmer credit, extend a credit to the concern which probably has put up a $5,000 or $7,000 building at that point although they had denied it to the agriculturist. That goes on all over Western Canada; I believe it to be the case in the east, wherever commodities are handled in large quantities and big sums of money are required. I quote that in substantiation of the statement I made that the viewpoint of the banking institutions of Canada is not as favourable to agriculture as it is to other industries. Of course those other industries may have two or three turn-overs in the course of a year, and that may be one of the reasons for the bank's policy towards them. But in the final analysis I am convinced, and I think all other hon. gentlemen are also, that agriculture is the surest source of wealth in Canada. Now we have a Government that does not seem to want to intervene in behalf of agriculture in that respect; I believe there is something lacking there. I believe that agriculture should demand that the influence of the Government should be used to see that equality prevails in the establishment of credits to commercial and agricultural enterprises alike.
I now wish to deal with the question of taxation. The axiom we should follow is

that those best able to bear taxation should pay it; and I believe that if we look into this matter closely we will come to the conclusion that the large banking institutions of Canada are not contributing as large a proportion to the taxes as the franchise extended to them by the Government warrants, although they are in better shape financially than other sections of the community. The statement issued with respect to the chartered banks of Canada up to March 31, is before me and a perusal of it would lead one to believe that these large institutions are concealing the value of their assets. I will give an example of what I mean, and because I use the names of certain banks I would not have the inference drawn that it is from any desire to discredit those particular institutions-I believe the same conditions prevail in all our banks. In the case of any business corporation it will be admitted that when in large urban centres a' central site is chosen and expensive buildings erected thereon, the value of the land and buildings is not stationary, but an increase in value follows. That does not appear to be the case in the bank statement; no matter for what.length of time a bank occupies a site it continues to send to the Government only the initial price paid for that land and the buildings erected upon it. For example, take the Royal Bank-which is considered one of the strongest if not the strongest bank in the Dominion at the present time. The figures for that institution are as follows:

Total Liability	 501,340,235
Assets over Liabilities	$ 42,407,916
Value of premises	 9,705,809
All hon. gentlemen who are familiar with large urban centres where the Royal Bank holds valuable property will realize that the price given in those figures is a very low estimate of the value of the sites and buildings which they possess. Now take the Bank of Montreal:

Total liabilities	 476,899,937
Assets over liabilities	$ 51,201,454
Value o£ premises	 5,550,000
The same condition obtains with respect to the Bank of Commerce, the Bank of Hamilton, the Imperial Bank and all the other banks. Now here is the comparison 
I wish to make: In the West we have the small city of Weyburn with a population of not more than 8,000. In that city there is a bank known as the Weyburn Security Bank, which has fifteen small branches located throughout the West. Many of these branches are established in villages, none of them in large populous centres and yet we find the figures sent in by the Weyburn Security Bank are $203,515 for fifteen branches, or an average value of $13,567. The initial price, or at least the price per site, of the Merchants Bank is $10,388, a less amount per site than that given by the little Weyburn Security Bank in the West. The Merchants Bank has its headquarters in a city which boasts a population of 750,000 and yet its average price is given as $3,250 less than the average site of t^e Weyburn Security Bank, located in m<v..y instances in places not having a larger population than 250. Something is wrong also when the Royal Bank shows a valuation of only $26 per site more than the little bank referred to. If it is a fact that these banking institutions are not sending in proper returns to the Government they should be obliged to live up to the law; otherwise what is the good of sending in the returns at all? If an organization or an individual were to go to the directors of the Bank of Montreal and ask them for the value of their buildings and sites they would probably place it at $50,500,000 rather than $5,550,000. If they have received profits of that nature from valuable franchises of the Dominion Government, I believe it is only right that investigation should be made so that they may be called upon to pay their fair share of the taxation of the country. There must be some reason why the returns are sent in in that manner.
Another illustration that I would give refers to land taxation. In our western country, and I believe in all the other provinces, we have the evil known as the land speculator, but particularly in the West, while even down in the province of New Brunswick I have heard complaints that the evil is prevalent and lands are being held out of use. In the part of the country in which my home is, when I went in there speculators, largely from the United States, held lands that they had purchased at from $1.50 to $3 an acre. Those lands at that time were not worth any more perhaps, but those speculators came in and bought them in sections, half townships and townships, and as the homesteads around were taken up and my neighbour and I-I use this

only as illustrative of what happened- made those vacant lands valuable, those speculators were able to sell at an increase in some instances as high as 1,500 per cent. I maintained in the first address I made in this House that that unearned increment is one of the means whereby this Government should receive taxation. What happens? Our big speculators come in from the United States and for an outlay of a few thousand dollars get in return hundreds of thousands of dollars, which they take back with them, and our Government stands aside and lets them do so. The State has created that wealth, and a portion of it should be taken for administering the affairs of the State. I think it is only logical and just that in Canada or in any other country where such conditions prevail the Government should step in and appropriate a certain portion of that unearned increment.
I read in the book which was quoted by the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cock-shutt) yesterday as an authority that agriculture every year loses approximately $125,000,000 because of destruction caused by vermin and insect pests. That is an enormous amount of money, and these large vacant areas are largely responsible, as any hon. gentleman who has lived in the West knows to be the fact, these large vacant areas are the breeding grounds of all the vermin and insect pests that prey upon our field crops. And those large vacant areas work this further hardship, that neighbours are a mile farther apart and 'have farther to go to church and to market; yet the settlers have to pay the taxes for the local improvements that enhance the value of these lands held by speculators. Every statement I make is applicable to the lands of the Canadian Pacific Railway and of its subsidiary companies. I think my suggestion can be worked out, and I am confident that the people of Canada will endorse a policy that will ensure a fair proportion of this unearned increment being appropriated for the use of the State. The taxation of these lands is a policy that we of the western provinces have to resort to simply because we have not any natural resources to fall back upon. We have been obliged for the purposes of provincial revenues to devise ways and means whereby taxes could be raised, and we have imposed a tax upon these people. Still they do not yet pay their fair proportion of the taxes. The residents have to pay the federal, provincial and municipal taxes, and now a sales tax is imposed, which increases the federal levy; but these speculators, who mostly live outside of Canada, escape the majority of these taxes, and pay no federal tax for the use of the land or for any unearned increment. I maintain that the federal authorities should oblige those speculators to leave a fair share of that unearned increment in this country, either in the form of straight taxes or of a substantial portion of the large profits they receive as a result of the enhanced prices of their land due to the efforts of the people in the community.
During the last ten or twelve years the provincial and federal governments have got much of their advice through commissions, but it is my opinion that the day of commissions is pretty nearly past. What Canada needs at the present ^ime is appraisers to go out and value the assets of the country-the assets of great institutions, to ascertain if they are paying their fair and equitable share of taxation. In the case of the civil servants here in Ottawa their Pay Sheets are taken as the basis for computing the taxes they shall pay. They are made of the same clay as the people interested in these large institutions, and the Government should be big enough to have men go out and place a value on them, so that they may be taxed as thoroughly as the civil servant. One should be treated the same as the other. I maintain that if appraisers are put on and institutions can show they are paying a fair share of taxation they will not suffer; but when men connected with those institutions decry the appointment of appraisers, that immediately raises a doubt in my mind as to whether they are really paying their fair and equitable share of taxation, because if they are they would have nothing to fear.
They would be delighted to have an investigation and to pay theip share of the taxes.

I would point out to my hon. friend from Haldimand (Mr. Lalor) that that is one of the planks in the platform of the Agrarian party, and I am pleased to know that he supports that plank. Despite all the lamentations over this platform, I find in the majority of cases wherever I have been speaking, whether here, in the country or on the floor of this House, invariably some plank in that platform is brought up which some one will endorse.

Now, on a number of platforms in the West preceding this session when being asked by members of my audience about the proposed tariff commission, I made this assertion-I do not wish to say this as endeavouring to prove that I am a prophet, for I am not, neither am I a descendant of a race of prophets-and it will be borne out, I believe, that all the tariff commission would amount to would be to fulfill the promise the Government had made to hold an inquiry, but that the evidence collected would be pigeon-holed. Such we find to be the case to-day. The people have demanded that the promises of the Government should be implemented to the fullest extent, and that following the work of that commission legislation should be brought before this House. We would like to know what the sentiment of the Government is in the matter of 'tariff revision, whether up or down. Just the bald statement that the Government stand for a protective platform is not good enough. The people demand from the Government, just as the Government have been demanding of the Opposition, a definite declaration - they want to know whether the revision is going to be up or down.

Will my hon. friend be good enough to tell me whether he accepts the policy of the Canadian Council of Agriculture to the effect that the British preference should be increased to fifty per cent and that free trade should be completed in this country inside of five years?
I am not sure whether the hon. gentleman is the same gentleman who asked that question yesterday.

A new seeker after
truth.

I have no hesitation in saying that that is our policy. I am not prepared to accept the view expressed by the hon. member for Brantford that if we were to have free trade with Great Britain it would mean free trade with the whole world. We h'ave a British preference at this time, but it does not affect the tariff in relation to other countries. In my humble opinion, it is absurd to say that if we have freedom of trade with Great Britain it must necessarily follow that we shall have free trade with the whole world.
The hon. member for Brantford asserted also that the policy as outlined by the hon. member for Marquette, my honoured leader, would be destructive to the interests of

the workingman of Canada; that our policy as laid down in the platform of the Canadian Council of Agriculture would work havoc and ruin to the Workingman as well as to the industries of Canada. Well, it was a case of simply making assertions without offering proof. Why the policy to which the hon. member for Brantford gives allegiance has already proved itself to be a failure. Take the case of Toronto, with the 20,000 men clamouring for bread; surely that in itself is condemnation of the present system. In a land in which the resources are so great and the agricultural possibilities so abundant, is there any reason why we should have starvation?
Will the hon. gentleman tell me how many are employed in free trade Britain?

I am not prepared to give the figures, but when coal strikes are on and other economic disturbances prevail, figures do not prove anything in any case. We do know, however, that Britain is recovering much more readily from her huge war debt than Canada is, and that may count for something.
I was making some reference to the sentiments expressed by the hon. member for Brantford. I believe that he asserted that the value of the exports of manufactured goods was in excess of the value of exports of agriculture. I asked the hon. gentleman at that time if it was not a fact that, taking say 5 bushels of wheat at a value of $1.50 a bushel, or $7.50, entering into the manufacture of a barrel of flour valued at $12-the only value coming under the head of manufacture being $4.50- I asked whether the whole value of the product $12 had not been credited to manufacture instead of only $4.50. Any computation on that basis would be quite unfair. If in such cases the price of the natural product were deducted from the value of the manufactured product, it would be found that the value of manufactured products exported does not compare with the value of the products of the farm, and the difference would be even greater if you added the products of the mines, the fisheries and the forests. The natural products of Canada are the wealth of Canada upon which the national debt rests and by and through which the national debt must be paid.
As a further illustration, take the case of hides. I have before me a letter written by my brother-in-law in which he asks

me if another brother-in-law had said anything to me about beef hides. He shipped to Brandon six hides and he got one cent a pound for them. After he had paid the express on these six beef hides he had $1.35 left-and Brandon is about 130 miles distant from his home. They say that every cloud has a silver lining. Well, the only silver lining I can see in this case is that if he is called upon to pay income tax next year it will not be very heavy. Six cow hides-and one dollar toward the price of a pair of shoes! You could load up a team with beef hides and you would not get enough from the sale of them to pay for the harness with which the load was drawn. That is agriculture, and if my hon. friend from Brantford wishes to take that as an illustration; if he takes the value of the hide when made into leather and into shoes and counts that as manufacture, and then asks the people of this House to believe that the value of manufactures exceeds the value of agricultural products, then I say that it is an enormity, an illustration used simply for the purposes of argument.
The Minister of Militia (Mr. Guthrie) has also done his best to make it appear throughout the country that this United Farmers' Organization is a very vicious institution. 'Likewise, the member for Brantford would make it appear that it was not a fact that the manufacturers of Canada had refused to sell to the United Grain Growers. Now, I happen to be a shareholder in that organization; I am proud to say that I was a shareholder in it when it was first started. This company has been doing my business; I am satisfied with the manner in which they are doing it, and that being the case I do not see that it is anybody else's business. The very fact that this company does a large volume of business proves that the people for whom they do business are satisfied with them.
The Minister of Militia, speaking in York or some place near Toronto, said that we were disloyal in not buying Canadian made implements. The privilege had been denied us at the time at which he spoke, but in the House he made reference to it, and we tried to give the hon. gentleman the evidence, possibly thinking that he did not have the full facts. But he said: "I do not wish to be interrupted." I do not know whether the hon. gentleman's sentiments are influenced by the signs which have been placed up by the Canadian Manufacturers, on one side: "Buy made-in-Canada goods," and on the other:
"Where will the revenue come from? " I read in the Estimates of the hon. gentleman's own department: "Customs duties on all imported stores and clothing, including material for the manufacture of ammunition, $40,000"-and this is the hon. gentleman who charges the farmers with being unpatriotic. Last year the item on this account was $50,000. Now why does the hon. gentleman go about the country trying to create prejudices, trying to make it appear that the farmers in the West, who were forced into this business in order to protect themselves from the avarice of financial institutions, are not acting properly, when the hon. gentleman himself was far more guilty of the very thing of which he charged us? But I wish to have it stated in Hansard that too much of this stuff is spoken, not in sincerity, but only on account of political prejudices, with a desire to make political capital. The people of the Dominion are anxiously looking for men who will speak in accordance with principles in which they believe and on which they act. That is, at least, what I am trying to do. I speak from a principle, and I have not yet reached the political stage where I would lose my sincerity to such an extent that I would try to take cheap political pat ty advantage of hon. gentlemen. That is beneath me, and, I believe it is beneath the policy of the group which I have the honour to represent.
Just a few words in closing. The minister rose to a very high tone in his closing remarks when he asked for the unity of the people of Canada. When he went to the manufacturers' associations, retail merchants' associations, Credit Men's associations and so on for advice, they advised him to discard the luxury and other taxes and to impose a sales tax. I wish to point out that the labouring man, the man who works in the mine or on the railway or on the farm, wears out more clothes and shoes than hon. gentlemen sitting in this chamber, and the. result will be that the sales tax will bear more heavily on those individuals, while the individuals who have a right and can afford to pay taxes on luxuries, are exempt. Had the minister gone to the Canadian Council of Agriculture, he would at least have heard the other side of the story and it is only fair to the great masses of the people of Canada that the minister, in his desire, which was, perhaps, an'earnest one, to get first hand information and advice, should have gone to all classes representative of the people of

the Dominion to ask for that advice. If, perchance, the minister has an opportunity another year of asking for advice. for the purposes of Government, I would advise him to go to that great organization, because we believe, and we have a right to believe, that we have in that great organization in the West, the Canadian Council of Agriculture, a body of men and women who are the equals intellectually of men and women in any other organization in this Dominion. But in all cases they have been despised and ignored by this Government, because they are the appointees of the plain people who think of these economic questions so much. When these people elect these men to do those things for them and this Government, sitting in high places, spurns and despises the advice which they give, not in a partisan spirit, these people have a right, perhaps, to repeat the sentiments that are sometimes sent out that this Government is representative only of the big interests of the Dominion of Canada. Not until all the people of Canada shall be taken into consideration, will faith again permeate the body politic. The minister asks for it in high tones; but he has not established a precedent himself, and I say, not in any spirit of antagonism, but in a desire to suggest something of the errors into which the Government has fallen and means whereby it can redeem itself largely in the eyes of the people, that it should not ignore the request of the plain people, hut should lend a sympathetic ear, because they are just as capable and wise as those belonging to other organizations, and in many" eases they seem to be used only as the dromedaries of taxation. The people object to that.

(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, if I rise at this stage of the debate, be assured that I do not intend to put forth new arguments to condemn as it should be condemned the policy of the present Administration; but as I occupy a seat in this Parliament in order to represent my constituents, I think it is my duty to express my most emphatic disapproval of the manner public business is administered by this Government. After having given us a real dance of the millions, after having completely destroyed Canadian credit by their extravagant expenditure, after having lead us to the very door of bankruptcy, our present administrators cannot find any other remedy to-day to help us out of the predicament in which they have placed us,

than to impose new taxes. Instead of practising the strictest economy, the present Government distribute gold by the handful, provided some of their friends are there to receive the lion's share.
These gentlemen talk of economy and of a wise administration of the public treasure only when it is proposed to assist some public undertaking, however meritorious, in the province of Quebec. If you ask these gentlemen to vote moneys for a post office, for the establishment of experimental farms or other similar works required in one of our counties, the answer is ever ready: "The treasury is empty"; but, should the proposal be to build a railway, or ships, or to increase the militia, oh! then, there is no hesitation in taking money out of the treasury and the debt continues to increase, to the despair of al. true patriots.
While listening to the speeches delivered, during the course of this debate, by the hon. minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton), by the right hon. Prime minister (Mr. Meighen), and by several others, one wonders if these gentlemen have not gone out of their minds. Instead of admitting that the State treasury is quite empty, that there is a large increase of our indebtedness at the end of each fiscal year, the present Government cry as loudly as possible that everything is all right and they continue cramming their friends.
The so-called tariff commission went travelling through the country during several months, and with a semblance of seriousness, they gathered the information as well as the suggestions which were available. Considering all these preparations, the electors throughout the country, were entitled to a revision of the tariff in view of improving present conditions.
Even the people in the rural districts were allured by the deceitful management of our Government leaders, and to mention a case with which I am well acquainted, and which I have taken especially to heart, I may refer to that of my friends, the tobacco growers of my district. Their situation is one of the most critical; some of them have yet on hand their tobacco harvest of 1919 and 1920, it is no unusual occurrence to meet farmers in my county who have a thousand, five thousand, ten thousand and even twenty thousand pounds of tobacco for sale and who are offered only ridiculously low prices. Yet, the hon. Minister of Finance has invited them to meet him in Montreal and even in Ottawa. They have explained to him the critical situation in

which they are placed, they have suggested to him remedies for their troubles. They had a right to expect that he would take their case into consideration and that something would be done to improve their fate; they had awaited the Budget with anxiety, and now they have been completely ignored by the Minister of Finance who evidently wishes to irritate them by depriving them of all hope for relief. In behalf of all these worthy farmers of whom advantage is being taken, in behalf of rfty good friends the tobacco growers of l'Assomption and Montcalm, I wish this evening to place on record my protest against the lack of pro- | tection given by the present Government to the interests of the agricultural class, and in behalf of the latter, I wish to repeat to my hon. friend the requests which I made when I submitted to him the representations made by the tobacco growers, in my county, and I would ask him to submit to the House, before the end of the session and without further delay, a measure to which I extend my support in advance, though it be on a protective basis because I declare myself for anything which may protect the farmer and the tobacco grower.
Such a measure should include the following provisions which sum up the fair claims of the tobacco growers of the country, that is to say:
I.	Increase the duty to one dollar a
pound on foreign tobacco, unstripped, and to one dollar and fifty cents on foreign tobacco, stripped.	*
II.	Make compulsory the destruction of the ribs stripped from the tobacco leaves, as required previous to 1917.
III.	Allow the producer to keep, for his
personal use, at least thirty-five pounds of leaf tobacco or other tobacco; give the same permission for each of his sons and his male servants.	.
IV.	Dispense growers of the requirement of securing a yearly permit and abolish the five cent duty per pound imposed on leaf tobacco, and if there must be a permit and a duty, to facilitate the collection of same by establishing an office to that effect in the post office of every locality where tobacco is being grown.
May I hope, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Finance will hear this appeal in the name of my electors? I entertain serious doubts in this respect. Nevertheless, it would show that really the minister is anxious to be fair towards the farmers of this country.
The hon. Minister of Finance and the Government of the day have heretofore
failed to implement their pledge to those who relied on the long advertised revision of the tariff. They have particularly omitted to procure relief to my good friends, the tobacco growers of l'Assomption and Montcalm; moreover, as I have not the least confidence in this Government of profiteers, I shall gladly vote against the motion of the Minister of Finance, giving my full support to the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's ;(Mr. Fielding).

(Translation). Mr. Speaker, I feel father embarrassed in addressing the House after all those splendid speeches. The hon. members on both sides, have spoken admirably on the subject of the Budget, and it so happens that, at two o'clock in the morning I am obliged to make a few remarks in all fairness to my electors. May I ask my hon. colleague to grant me their attention for a few minutes?
(Translation). Hear, hear.

(Translation.)
When one is in business, Mr. Speaker, it is necessary at times to take stock. Merchants, manufacturers, business men and even to professional men examine the state of their business every year, and this is what I mean to do this evening, as a politician.
I have seen many a thing in my time- unfortunately I am getting old. When hon. Mr. Mackenzie came to power, and this is a long time ago, I was a young man, yet I was interested in politics. He came to power in 1874, and administered public affairs until 1878. He was a freetrader. He was an honest man, a man of strong principles. No one ever doubted the sincerity of the late Hon. Mr. Mackenzie. Amongst other important things which he did, was the institution of the Supreme Court. He gave the people the ballot system, he continued the construction of railways which had been begun. We had just had the amazing scandal, the Pacific scandal, and I remember well the words of the Conservative leader of the time: "These hands are clean." He spoke the truth. The late Sir John Macdonald, an honest man, a most distinguished politician, had not taken any part in this, extraordinary scandal, this colossal scandal, for which his friends were responsible. One had received a large amount, another had received a smaller one; there were quite a few whose hands were not clean. That is why Sir John Macdonald de-

dared: "My hands are dean." And I believe it was true. The hon. Mr. Mackenzie assumed the duties of office and performed these until 1878. He was a free-trader, and decidedly so. The people did not approve of his administration. Sir John Macdonald, who was cumiing, took advantage of the situation to ask for protection; the national policy which he had always refused to give. He had been a free-trader at first, but seeing that his opponent was also a free-trader, he said to himself: This may help me in getting into power, I am going to declare myself a protectionist. He won the elections wiih a large majority, assumed power ana governed until his death, in 1891. He was replaced by Sir John Abbott, a distinguished lawyer from Montreal, and one that held a high reputation, an honest man who did not live very long. He did not have time to do much. He was succeeded by Sir John Thompson, who was a Catholic; and who kept the reins of power until his death which occurred in England. Great Britain furnished the ship which brought his body home to Canada. On the ship's arrival at Halifax, there was another scandal and a very extraordinary one. I remember taking part in elections at that time when we were speaking of the famous scandal which had occurred on the occasion of the death of Sir John Thompson. The friends of the deceased managed to spend a considerable amount of money for his funeral. The pall bearers were given each a new pair of shoes, worth fifteen dollars and a silk hat. Generally, when you go to a funeral, before leaving your house you take your hat along with you, and you do not expect a new hat to he given to you at the deceased's house, on that occasion, you had to wear a new silk hat. Usually you give a pair of gloves to each one of the pall bearers; but this time you required twelve pairs, for each pall bearer. There were roses also. Well, it is the custom to give roses to newly-wed couples, but on the occasion of a funeral, you usually give a wreath or a few flowers. At any rate, they spent $2,000 worth of flowers for this funeral, the total cost of which amounted to $12,500. When we told the people that they had spent that much for a funeral, they would not believe it; we had to bring them the Hansard and let them read the evidence thus brought out; then they realized that we were telling the truth. So much said for the funeral of Sir John Thompson. He was succeeded by Sir Mackenzie Bowell, who was an honest man.

men as Mr. Joly, once premier of the province- of Quebec. He gathered the Prime Ministers from every province and thus formed a very, strong cabinet.
For the Department of Agriculture, he chose a most practical man, Hon. Mr. Fisher, who died recently. He was a man of great experience. He knew the difference between a duck and a goose. The former Minister of Agriculture, Mr. Montague, coming to a farm-yard one day, said to the farmer's wife: "Madame, what a fine goose you have there!" "Sir," she replied, "this is not a goose, it is a duck." He did not know the difference between a goose and a duck. Mr. Fisher knew better. With men of such worth, well-known men of high reputation, in Sir Wilfrid's Laurier's Cabinet, not the first year, because there was a small deficit, but each subsequent year, there was a great surplus at the end of the fiscal year, whilst the other gentlemen, the previous administrators, had deficits, and large deficits, Mr. Speaker, this proves what men of worth, talent and integrity Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his colleagues were; they administered the country wisely, prudently, rightly, and with the greatest success.
The Hon. Mr. Mackenzie was somewhat obstinate; he was a Scotchman. He was advised by friends, at that time, to change the tariff, but he did not want to do so. He was a free trader, and held firm to his principles. That brought his defeat. Sometimes I hear hon. members on the Government side trying bo recall the past in order to prove that Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his friends were free traders; but, these gentlemen are only quoting things that happened before Laurier came to power. They quote Sir Richard Cartwright, he was a free trader. Some of his friends were free traders, but Sir Wilfrid always refused to adopt that policy. He adopted the policy of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) which was of a happy medium, and that policy is mine also. I regret not being able to follow the arguments which our hon. friends on the ministerial side are trying to bring forward, but I prefer adopting the same argument as the hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) whom I trust. I listened to him to-day with great pride. There were several candidates at the large convention. We struggled hard before we made our choice. Hon. Mr. Graham was one of the candidates, there was the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens, he is not a first-
comer, he is an extraordinary man; we had the leader of the Opposition who was chosen in preference to all; neither is the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie.) a first-comer, and he also was there; but we needed a leader in Parliament, we could not have a family of leaders, we had to choose one only, and I think we chose the best. The hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's is here, he has shown what he could do during fifteen years, and we want him for our Minister of Finance at the first opportunity. I assure you that it is not an easy matter to get millions from the hon. member. He was very strict. His friends . thought so, because he did not unfasten the purse-strings very readily. One wants unreasonable things sometimes, and asks for them just the same, then, sulks and murmurs when it is impossible to obtain what has been asked; but, I assure you that one must be careful with the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's; one must be there early to get something; but let us honour him for that, honour is due to this method of managing the public funds. He has proven his worth, he is highly reputed as a financial man, and we want him to continue the work he has started with such success.
When Sir Wilfrid came into power and the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's had given us the tariff, manufactures were built as if by magic. My county is a manufacturing county, it is the county of Jacques-Cartier. There are several manufactures in the county of Jacques-Cartier, and they were all prosperous; industries were most prosperous during Sir Wilfrid Laurier's and the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's time. Manufactures rose amongst us as quickly as mushrooms. In less time than it takes to say it, a big chimney, a large manufacture was built; and, Mr. Speaker, were you to visit the county of Jacques-Cartier and see what is being done at Sainte Anne, Point Claire, Dixie, Valois, Lachine, Dorval, St. Pierre-aux-Liens, Cote Saint Paul, Emhrd, Saint Gabriel, you would be most astonished to see the great number of manufactures that have been erected in that district.
Then you go to Cartierville? you come to Saint-Laurent, to park Amherst, to Bordeaux ; manufactures and very, prosperous manufacturers. And if ever the hon. member for Prince, who is our leader, wanted to adopt a policy capable of hurting these industries, I would vote against him. But there is no danger; he is of the good school.

He attended the school of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the school of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's, that is enough. I am certain he will never swerve from the proper course, from the golden mean, which would permit success to the manufacturer and give the working class, the artisan, the workman, bread for their families. I am certain he will never swerve from that course, should he try to do so, D. A. Lafor-tune, member for Jacques-Cartier, would be against him. But no danger of that.
The agricultural class was most prosperous during the fifteen years of the last Administration-Sir Wilfrid Laurier knew its needs, and his followers knew what their electors needed. As for myself, I have lived in the country for the last thirty-five years, cultivating farms at Saint-Laurent, and under the Liberal Administration I have been proud and happy; but since the fall of Sir Wilfrid and his friends, distress, want prevail'. In former time, the name of Sir Wilfrid Laurier meant prosperity; that of the hon. member for King's (Sir Robert Borden) and his successor spelt wretchedness. They had the same tariff, they had the same elements to deal with; but the boss was not the same. He had promised to settle the burning school question which Sir 1 John A. Macdonald, Sir MacKenzie Bowell, Sir Charles Tupper, Sir John Thompson, all the Conservative leaders that are no more, had promised, but failed to settle. Mr. Laurier succeeded to settle this question, not completely, but to the satisfaction of the episcopate, to the satisfaction of His Holiness Leo XIII, who said to the faithful-I advise you to accept this settlement, it is not complete; I would have desired to see it more satisfactory to the Catholics, but under the circumstances, accept what is given and pray God you may obtain the rest.
This question has dissappeared from the field of discussion. All are content, and I pay my tribute to the Canadian clergy for having, by their acceptance of that settlement, put an end to the then existing trouble. Since that day, there is no hell for the Liberals, we do not hear any more that the heavens are blue, that hell is red (the colours of the two parties of that day), and the clergy has done justice to us in putting us on an equal footing. Those days are ended.
I remember going once into a church, in the district of Three-Rivers. The parish priest ascended the pulpit and said: "My
children, be careful, there are Liberals today in the village, in the parish; do not listen to them, listen to your priest. You know that hell is red, and that heaven is blue." I need not tell you that we left the church not over-pleased for having been treated in that way. We were going there to do our duty, to preach peace, concord, to make known the policy of the Liberal party; we were not expecting such treatment. But, all credit to the clergy now! Those things are of the past. Now, the Liberals are treated like the Conservatives and vice versa. We have nothing to complain of.
It had been said that contracts would be given to the lowest tenderers, and Sir Wilfrid, jealous of his word, had a law passed providing that for all cases of contracts of over $5,000, tenders should be invited, and that all such should be given to the lowest bidder. When you see the hon. Minister of Marine giving $78,000,000 contracts without tenders; when you see, I say, the Minister of Marine giving contracts for 75 or 78 million dollars without tenders-I will not abuse him, he is a former Liberal', let us respect him; but I will tell him that he has violated the law put on the statute book by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, which prohibits contracts being given without tenders in matters of more than $5,000. That law, the hon. minister has had occasion to see it, to read it, to get acquainted with it, but he did not respect it-let him allow me to say that he does not respect the laws that are on the statute books, he over-rides them, he does not mind them. He is king and master in his department, but let me say to him-"Sir, this is not the way the laws of the land should be observed."
There has been put in the contracts a clause which did not exist before-to the effect that the workman's salary should be respected by the contractors and all subcontractors, and that the recipient of a contract, would be responsible for the workman's salary. It was not that way before. A contract was given to Peter, Peter would transfer it to Baptiste, Baptiste to Paul, and in the end the workmen did not know whom to apply to for their pay and they lost it.
There are now in the agreements a clause which protects the labourers, and that is what we had said.
We have built a great number of post offices. The Montreal post office was in a wretched condition, as well as in other places; every public building was neglected,

and we had to provide for a great number of post offices and for repairing those which existed. That cost very dear but notwithstanding the expenses incurred for those large undertakings there was always a surplus at the end of the year.
In Montcalm, I had succeeded with great difficulty to get the consent of the 'honourable Minister of Finance to give me a post office. I had difficulties because he thought that the population was not sufficiently great, and that the business of the community was not sufficiently large. I proved to Mr. Laurier and the Minister of Finance that a post office in Montcalm was necessary and I got it. What happened? A site was bought and paid for; I had specifications prepared and I was ready to ask for tenders when the general elections were held and my post office was left there. At the present time, it is the cats and dogs that occupy the site; the specifications remained in the pigeon holes and we have never been able since that time to get a post office built. I am not sorry for it, because I have obtained from the voters of Montcalm a promise that if I could get a post office built there, they would give it my name, but, let them not do it, and I will have it built myself and my name shall be there; that post office will be the work of the next administration. They will ask for tenders and the Saint-Jacqueis post office will be built, and I shall he glad to have contributed to it.
The Hon. Mr. Laurier created two large provinces, and, if we have the honour now to have so many distinguished men from Alberta and from Saskatchewan, to whom are we indebted? It is thanks to Mr. Laurier. It is the government of that time who gave us an opportunity to bring to this House so many distinguished men from the West. There is something more to do at the present time. There is the great NorthWest Territory to open, and we shall do it when we have a Liberal government, and it will not be long now.
The hon.
